**Summary.** This paper proposes algebraic surgery as a method to efficiently implement logical measurements for qLDPC codes on neutral-atom quantum processors. By leveraging the inherent algebraic structure of the codes, the authors achieve constant shuttling depth and faster cycle times compared to general graph-based approaches. This demonstrates that algebraic insights can simplify physical implementation and expand the accessible logical operations on trapped-atom hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly tackles the physical realization bottleneck in quantum computation by showing how abstract algebraic structures can be mapped onto physical hardware constraints (like shuttling depth) in a computationally efficient manner.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of implementing high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes on physical quantum processors by developing hardware-efficient logical measurement protocols.

**Main result.** Algebraic surgery provides a method to achieve constant shuttling depth for parallel logical measurements, significantly outperforming general graph-based schedules in simulated cycle times.

**Method.** The authors introduce algebraic surgery, a structured technique applied to lifted product codes, which co-designs logical measurements, auxiliary codes, and atom shuttling to preserve underlying algebraic symmetries.

**Model / system.** The physical platform modeled is a reconfigurable atom array using neutral atoms, where connectivity and operations are mediated by controlled atom shuttling via AODs.

**Key observables.** Shuttling depth ($\delta_{	ext{shuttle}}$), cycle time comparison (algebraic vs. graph-based), Logical Error Rates (LERs), and physical qubit overhead.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis is sensitive to explicit layout assumptions for achieving constant shuttling depth, and performance is benchmarked across varying code sizes and error probabilities ($p$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The constant shuttling depth relies on explicit layout assumptions, and the code-capacity results for finite codes do not establish a true error threshold.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the cyclic LP code structure and the comparison of shuttling depths between algebraic and graph-based surgeries. Figure 3 compares shuttling and gate times for syndrome extraction across different code types.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the need for hardware-efficient logical operations to introducing algebraic surgery, benchmarking its performance against existing graph-based methods in terms of time and depth, and finally analyzing the resulting code capacity and error rates.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Reconfigurable atom arrays provide a promising platform for high-rate quantum low-density parity-check codes, but their computational advantage depends on whether logical operations can be implemented without incurring prohibitive shuttling and space overheads. We introduce algebraic surgery for lifted product codes, co-designing the logical measurements, auxiliary codes, and atom shuttling to enable hardware-efficient Pauli-product measurements. These protocols provide flexible logical addressability subject to the cyclic-symmetry constraint, enabling a broad class of parallel logical measurements, including canonical logical operators with heavily overlapping physical supports and joint measurements within or between code blocks even with different lift sizes, while achieving constant shuttling depth on neutral-atom processors under explicit layout assumptions. In a representative hardware-model benchmark, a cycle supporting 33 parallel canonical logical measurements is about $2\times$ faster than the compared single-observable graph-based surgery schedules, with competitive qubit overhead. These shuttling and circuit-level simulations confirm that the algebraic structure of quantum low-density parity-check codes can be used not only to reduce space overhead, but also to simplify physical implementation and expand the set of efficiently accessible logical operations on neutral-atom processors.

</details>

**Summary.** This work reports on the successful creation and detailed characterization of negatively charged boron vacancy color centers in bulk h-BN using high-energy helium ion irradiation. By employing ODMR and PL spectroscopy, the authors confirmed the spin properties of the defect and measured its physical depth. This research advances the use of 2D materials for solid-state quantum memory and sensing applications.

**Why it may be interesting.** The $	ext{B}_{	ext{V}}^-$ center acts as a solid-state spin qubit candidate. The detailed characterization of its spin Hamiltonian parameters ($D, E, \gamma$) and its integration into a robust fabrication protocol are highly relevant for quantum information research.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper focuses on demonstrating the reliable fabrication and characterizing the negatively charged boron vacancy ($	ext{B}_{	ext{V}}^-$) color center in bulk hexagonal boron nitride ($	ext{h-BN}$).

**Main result.** The authors successfully confirmed the creation of $	ext{B}_{	ext{V}}^-$ centers using characteristic photoluminescence and optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) measurements.

**Method.** The research combines experimental techniques like high-energy $	ext{He}^+$ ion irradiation, PL, and ODMR with theoretical modeling (SRIM) to characterize the defect.

**Model / system.** The system is the $	ext{B}_{	ext{V}}^-$ color center in bulk $	ext{h-BN}$. The electronic structure is modeled by a Hamiltonian involving zero-field splitting ($D$) and orthorhombic splitting ($E$), which governs its spin $S=1$ behavior in a magnetic field.

**Key observables.** Photoluminescence (PL) spectrum (peak at 800–850 nm), Zeeman shift in ODMR resonance lines, and the depth profile of the color center along the c-axis.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Zero-field splitting parameter ($D \approx 3.48 	ext{ GHz}$), orthorhombic splitting ($E \approx 50 	ext{ MHz}$), and the measured resonance width ($180 	ext{ MHz}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary discrepancy noted is that the experimental depth of the vacancy is greater than the depth predicted by standard SRIM modeling, suggesting unaccounted physical processes like ion channeling.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the crystal structure, the energy level diagram of the $	ext{B}_{	ext{V}}^-$ center, and schematics of the confocal microscope setup used for ODMR measurements.

**Paper structure.** The paper follows a structure of problem definition (need for 2D color centers), experimental demonstration (irradiation, PL, ODMR), quantitative analysis (measuring Zeeman shifts and depth), and comparison with theoretical modeling.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

While color centers in diamond and other three-dimensional crystals are nowadays key elements of several types of sensors, color centers in two-dimensional materials are rapidly developing and promise high-tech applications. One of the interesting centers in 2D materials is the negatively charged boron vacancy in hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN), which has already shown some potential for magnetometry, but the reliable creation of boron vacancies remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate the fabrication of negatively charged boron vacancy color centers in bulk h-BN via implantation of helium ions at ~1 MeV, as confirmed by characteristic photoluminescence and optically detected magnetic resonance. The resonance has a width of 180 MHz and exhibits the expected Zeeman shift of the resonance lines. The depth of the color center along the c-axis of the h-BN crystal was measured and compared with predictions from Stopping and Range of Ions in Matter modeling. The experimental value and the modeled prediction are consistent within the reported uncertainties, as their 1σ intervals overlap, although the experiment shows a greater depth and a wider distribution.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper experimentally establishes a fundamental tradeoff inequality linking local quantum resources (maximum coherence) and global quantum resources (quantum mutual information) in bipartite quantum states. Using entangled photons, the authors demonstrate that these resources are complementary, showing that enhancing one necessarily constrains the other. This provides crucial physical insight into the resource management within quantum networks.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides concrete experimental evidence for fundamental resource constraints in quantum information, linking local properties (coherence) to global correlations (QMI) in a way that has implications for quantum network design.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates and experimentally demonstrates a fundamental tradeoff relationship between local quantum resources (measured by maximum coherence) and global quantum resources (measured by quantum mutual information).

**Main result.** A tradeoff inequality is established showing that the sum of local maximum coherence and quantum mutual information is bounded by a definitive upper limit. This implies that local and global quantum resources are mutually exclusive, meaning enhancing one necessarily limits the other.

**Method.** The authors use quantum state tomography on experimentally generated entangled photon pairs to measure various quantum resource quantities. They compare experimental measurements against theoretically derived tradeoff inequalities.

**Model / system.** The study uses an optical quantum system employing polarization degrees of freedom of entangled photon pairs generated via Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC). The system is analyzed for both pure and mixed bipartite quantum states.

**Key observables.** Local maximum coherence ($C_{\max}(ho_A) + C_{\max}(ho_B)$) and Quantum Mutual Information ($I(ho_{AB})$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The tradeoff inequality itself, $C_{\max}(ho_A) + C_{\max}(ho_B) + I(ho_{AB}) \leq \log_2(d_A d_B)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the basis-independent measure of maximum coherence, $C_{\max}(ho)$, and the derived inequality holds with equality if and only if the state is pure.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the local-global tradeoff curve, showing the relationship between local coherence and QMI for both pure and mixed states, comparing experimental data points to theoretical bounds.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the concept of the local-global tradeoff, then details the experimental setup using entangled photons. It derives the general tradeoff inequality, experimentally verifies this inequality for pure states, and analyzes how mixed states fall below the theoretical bound due to entropy.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The interconversion among different quantum resources has attracted considerable attention, exemplified by the tradeoff between coherence and entanglement. However, the relationship between local and global quantum resources remains largely unexplored. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a local global tradeoff in quantum resources, quantified respectively by the local maximum coherence and the quantum mutual information. Our experiments show that the sum of the local maximum coherence and the quantum mutual information is bounded by a definitive upper limit. These results not only establish a fundamental tradeoff inequality, but also provide direct experimental evidence of the complementarity between local and global quantum resources. Moreover, our findings reveal an important constraint in quantum networks: the local quantum resources available at individual nodes and the global quantum resources of the network are mutually exclusive, implying that enhancing one necessarily limits the other.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors present a microwave-driven, reservoir- and measurement-free method to initialize semiconductor spin qubits into a target singlet state. By exploiting spin-charge physics near a Pauli blockade, they achieve high-fidelity initialization using only fixed microwave pulse sequences. This establishes a crucial, scalable control primitive for building large quantum processors.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides an experimentally validated, solid-state method for state preparation that circumvents major scaling bottlenecks in quantum computing architectures, directly relevant to solid-state quantum information processing.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing scalable methods for initializing semiconductor spin qubits without relying on complex, hard-to-distribute local reservoirs or measurement feedback.

**Main result.** A fixed-sequence microwave initialization protocol was demonstrated, achieving a high singlet-associated charge outcome probability of 99.4% and establishing a scalable control primitive for spin-qubit processors.

**Method.** The protocol uses a fixed sequence of microwave and baseband pulses to drive the system through the triplet manifold, enabling conversion to the singlet charge state.

**Model / system.** The work uses silicon spin qubits in an industrially fabricated Si/SiGe quantum-dot device, operating near the (1, 3)–(0, 4) Pauli-blockade transition.

**Key observables.** Singlet-associated charge outcome probability ($P_S$), Rabi oscillation visibility, and charge-signal difference (CSD) measurements.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Initialization time scale ($\approx 12 \mu	ext{s}$ initially, projecting sub-microsecond), and the singlet-triplet mixing time ($	au_{mix}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method relies on singlet-triplet physics within the Pauli spin blockade regime, suggesting applicability to other platforms with similar physics.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the spin-charge spectrum, the initialization cycle energy schematic, Rabi oscillations, and the dependence of initialization probability on repetition number and pulse parameters.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from characterizing the physical system and coherent control (Rabi oscillations) to detailing the fixed-sequence initialization protocol, analyzing its repetition dependence, and finally establishing its viability as a scalable control primitive.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Scalable quantum processors require repeated qubit initialization throughout large arrays. In semiconductor spin qubits, fast initialization commonly relies on local reservoir access or measurement-based feedback, requiring dedicated infrastructure that becomes increasingly difficult to distribute as processors scale. Here, we demonstrate reservoir- and measurement-free initialization of a silicon spin-qubit pair in an industrially fabricated Si/SiGe quantum-dot device using a fixed sequence of microwave and baseband pulses. Odd spin-parity states relax to the singlet charge state, whereas blocked even spin-parity states are microwave-driven through the triplet manifold and subsequently converted to the singlet by singlet-triplet mixing and charge hybridization. Repeated cycles produce the singlet-associated charge outcome with a median probability of 99.4% across the sampled preparation states, while exchange spectroscopy independently verifies mapping to the target $|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle$ operational state. Microwave spectroscopy and time-domain measurements identify the dark-state-limited single-cycle transfer and the subsequent blockade-lifting dynamics that set the initialization time scale. The demonstrated pumping sequence uses approximately $12\,μ\mathrm{s}$ of microwave bursts and mixing dwells, while we project sub-microsecond initialization under improved device conditions. These results establish fixed-sequence microwave initialization as a scalable control primitive for semiconductor spin-qubit processors, based on singlet-triplet physics that can be adapted to platforms with suitable Pauli-blockade transitions.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper investigates the complex phase behavior of a binary mixture of spin-1 BECs, demonstrating the existence of a novel 'mixed-bubble' ground state using mean-field theory. The authors show that the stability of this phase depends critically on the applied magnetic field, offering a pathway to engineer specific spatial mixing patterns in quantum gas systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a detailed theoretical mechanism for stabilizing complex, non-trivial spatial structures (mixed bubbles) in spinor BEC mixtures purely through mean-field interactions, which is crucial for designing quantum simulators.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To theoretically demonstrate the emergence of a mixed-bubble state in a binary mixture of spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) using mean-field theory.

**Main result.** The study shows that the mixed-bubble phase exists in the ground state phase diagram, contrasting with simpler predictions, and that a metastable uniformly-mixed state can transition into this mixed-bubble state via local perturbations.

**Method.** The analysis employs mean-field theory, solving coupled Gross-Pitaevskii equations and minimizing the total energy/Gibbs free energy to map out the ground state phase diagram.

**Model / system.** The system is a binary mixture of spin-1 $^{7}{m{Li}}$ and $^{23}{m{Na}}$ BECs in a uniform trap, governed by mean-field interactions and subject to external magnetic fields.

**Key observables.** Ground-state phase diagram ($ar{n}_1$ vs $ar{n}_2$), density distributions ($ho_j(r)$), magnetization profiles ($\mathbf{F}^{(j)}(r)$), and the Gibbs free energy $g(R)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Magnetic field strength ($B_z$), average densities ($ar{n}_1, ar{n}_2$), and the mixing ratio ($R$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the system is in the thermodynamic limit, zero total magnetization ($\sum_j \mathbf{f}^{(j)}(r) = 0$), and relies on mean-field approximations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the phase diagram showing three distinct phases (mixed-bubble, uniformly-mixed, totally-separated) as a function of $B_z$, and show density/magnetization profiles characterizing these different spatial domain structures.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the theoretical framework using the GP equations, analyzes the energy landscape via the Gibbs free energy $g(R)$ to predict phase stability, and finally uses dynamic arguments to show the transition between the metastable uniform state and the mixed-bubble state.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In mean-field theory, the ground state of a two-component Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) in a uniform system is either uniformly mixed or totally separated. Beyond-mean-field effects introduce an additional phase, the mixed-bubble state, in which the two components remain mixed within one of the separated domains. Here we show that a mixed-bubble state can emerge in a binary mixture of spin-1 ${}^{7}{\rm{Li}}$ and ${}^{23}{\rm{Na}}$ BECs even within the mean-field framework. We further demonstrate the existence of a metastable uniformly-mixed state, which undergoes a transition to the mixed-bubble state triggered by a local perturbation.

</details>

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a rigorous, generalized framework for quantum-inspired sensing limits in classical optics, showing deep structural parallels between classical measurement theory and quantum information theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper develops a general formalism to establish universal bounds on the performance of optical sensing, independent of the specific optical hardware used.

**Main result.** The derived optical measurement formalism is nearly identical to the quantum one, yielding a universal uncertainty principle that controls measurement performance for any passive optical system.

**Method.** The authors adapt the quantum Cramér-Rao bound methodology, deriving a classical Fisher information for the optical case using a Pixel Operator Measure (POM) formalism.

**Model / system.** The analysis applies to general passive optical systems, including imagers and interferometers, modeling the measurement as an expectation value derived from the electric field at the focal plane.

**Key observables.** Fisher information ($I_	heta$), measurement uncertainty ($\sigma^2$), and the state density matrix ($\hat{ho}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Aperture diameter ($D$), wavelength ($\lambda$), noise variance ($\sigma^2$), and the parameter to be estimated ($	heta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes paraxial fields, a simple canonical detector response, and that electronics noise is the dominant source, independent of the field state.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 schematically depicts a general optical system flow: Aperture -> Linear Optical Material -> Photodetectors.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from establishing the general formalism and the POM measurement description, derives the optical Cramér-Rao bound, and then applies this bound to specific sensing problems like wavefront aberration and depth estimation, comparing results to the quantum limit.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Inspired by results in quantum information, we report the development of a formalism for optical sensing which abstracts the details of specific optical systems and allows us to form general bounds on measurement based only on the quantity to be measured. We find a universal bound that controls the performance of any passive optical system regardless of the technology used to construct it and that this bound is attained by a unique measurement scheme for each quantity of interest. Shockingly, our optical formalism is nearly identical to the quantum formalism, with essentially the same notions of the state to be measured and the operation of the measurement, along with an accompanying uncertainty principle.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper provides an algebraic framework to characterize the high-dimensional spatial entanglement of biphotons generated by SPDC using LG-pumped beams. By decomposing the process into beam-splitter and squeezing operations, the authors derive the Schmidt number as a function of the pump mode indices. This offers a deep theoretical understanding of entanglement dimensionality and associated conservation laws in structured light quantum sources.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous, mathematically unified description of high-dimensional entanglement resources generated optically, which is crucial for designing quantum communication protocols based on structured light.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to develop an algebraic framework to characterize the complex spatial-mode entanglement generated in biphotons via Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC) when the pump beam uses higher-order Laguerre-Gaussian (LG) modes.

**Main result.** The authors derive an analytical expression for the Schmidt number, showing how the radial and azimuthal indices of the LG pump modes govern the dimensionality of the spatial entanglement. They also establish conservation laws when the pump beam radius matches the crystal correlation width.

**Method.** The core method involves factorizing the SPDC process into a spatial-mode beam-splitter transformation followed by a spatial two-mode squeezing operation, analyzed in the transverse wavevector space.

**Model / system.** The system is the biphoton state $|\Psi_{N^-}^{N+}angle$ generated in an SPDC process using a higher-order LG-pumped beam. The analysis utilizes the LG-mode basis and sum/difference coordinates for the signal and idler photons.

**Key observables.** Biphoton spatial-mode entanglement, Schmidt number ($K$), Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM), and the total spatial mode number ($N$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Pump-beam radius ($w_p$), crystal-induced correlation width ($w_-$), and the squeezing parameter ($\xi = \ln(w_p/w_-)$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The pump light is assumed to be monochromatic, CW, and collimated, and the analysis often assumes degenerate wavelengths.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from the general Hamiltonian description of the SPDC state, develops an algebraic factorization into beam-splitter and squeezing operations, analyzes the resulting conservation laws in different regimes ($\xi=0$ vs $\xi
eq 0$), and culminates in deriving asymptotic expressions for the Schmidt number.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

High-dimensional spatial entanglement generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) provides a powerful resource for quantum information processing, yet its mode structure becomes increasingly complex when the pump occupies a higher-order Laguerre--Gaussian (LG) mode. Here, we develop an algebraic framework for characterizing biphoton spatial-mode entanglement by factorizing LG-pumped SPDC into a spatial-mode beam-splitter transformation followed by spatial two-mode squeezing. By choosing the biphoton LG basis radius as the geometric mean of the pump-beam radius and the crystal-induced correlation width, we obtain a natural modal basis in which the two operations can be treated separately. When the pump-beam radius matches the correlation width, spatial squeezing vanishes, and the two circular-mode components of the pump are independently conserved across the signal and idler photons, leading to conservation of both orbital angular momentum and the total spatial mode number. We further derive an analytical expression for the Schmidt number for arbitrary LG pump modes and squeezing strengths, revealing how the radial and azimuthal pump indices govern the dimensionality of the spatial entanglement. This algebraic characterization provides a unified description of the mode structure, conservation laws, and entanglement dimensionality of higher-order-LG-pumped SPDC.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper establishes a precise geometric criterion for determining when multiple quantum measurements (POVMs) on a qubit can be performed simultaneously (jointly measured). It proves that for coplanar measurements, joint measurability is equivalent to the perimeter of the convex hull of the associated Bloch vectors being at most 4. The methodology combines quantum information theory with advanced convex optimization techniques.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides fundamental geometric constraints on the compatibility of quantum measurements, which is crucial for designing quantum information protocols and understanding measurement limitations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper determines the necessary and sufficient conditions for the joint measurability (compatibility) of multiple unbiased binary qubit Positive Operator-Valued Measures (POVMs).

**Main result.** For coplanar POVMs, joint measurability is equivalent to the perimeter of the convex closure of their Bloch vectors being less than or equal to 4.

**Method.** The problem is reformulated as a convex optimization problem involving minimizing a norm subject to linear constraints derived from the POVM structure.

**Model / system.** The system involves unbiased binary qubit POVMs, which are characterized by their corresponding Bloch vectors $\mathbf{a}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$. The analysis focuses on the geometric arrangement of these vectors.

**Key observables.** The Bloch vectors $\mathbf{a}_i$, the perimeter of the convex hull $\text{conv}\{\pm \mathbf{a}_i\}$, and the function $L(\mathbf{a}_1, \dots, \mathbf{a}_n)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimension of the space (2D vs 3D) and the value of the perimeter relative to 4 (or $L_n \le 1$ in general).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis initially focuses on the case where the Bloch vectors are coplanar ($\mathbb{R}^2$), and later relies on general convex optimization theory.

**Figures summary.** Not specified in the notes.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem equivalence using minimization techniques, derives the condition for the coplanar case using geometric arguments involving the convex hull, and confirms the result by solving the underlying convex optimization problem.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

An unbiased qubit positive operator-valued measure (POVM) can be uniquely expressed in terms of the Bloch vector. We prove that for POVMs with coplanar Bloch vectors, they are jointly measurable if and only if the perimeter of the convex closure of Bloch vectors is less than or equal to 4. Moreover, as a corollary, we give an affirmative answer to the conjecture suggested by [Andrejic-Kunjwal 2020] on the existence of a joint device for POVMs whose Bloch vectors lie on the same circle.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper determines the minimum number of quantum copies required to estimate the purity of an unknown quantum state with high accuracy using only incoherent measurements. By developing both non-adaptive and adaptive estimators and proving corresponding lower bounds via Gaussian testing, the authors establish the optimal copy complexity scaling for this quantum estimation problem.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides rigorous complexity bounds for a fundamental quantum estimation task, showing the quantitative advantage of adaptive measurement strategies in the high-precision limit, which is crucial for designing practical quantum protocols.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the fundamental task of estimating the purity ($	ext{tr}(ho^2)$) of an unknown quantum state $ho$ using measurements on multiple copies.

**Main result.** It establishes the optimal copy complexity for this estimation using incoherent measurements, showing a minimum complexity of $\Theta\left(\min\left\{ rac{d}{\varepsilon^2} + rac{d^{3/2}}{\varepsilon}, rac{d^2}{\varepsilon} + rac{\sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon^2}ight\}ight)$.

**Method.** The authors develop and analyze both non-adaptive and adaptive estimation algorithms, deriving lower bounds by reducing the problem to distinguishing between Gaussian distributions via noisy linear queries.

**Model / system.** The system involves an unknown quantum state $ho$ of dimension $d$. The measurement process is restricted to incoherent measurements on multiple copies, contrasting with ideal collective measurements.

**Key observables.** Purity ($	ext{tr}(ho^2)$), the estimated purity $\hat{P}$, and the measurement outcomes $y$ from POVMs.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The relative error $\varepsilon$, the dimension $d$, and the number of copies $n$. The analysis distinguishes between regimes like $\varepsilon = o(1/d)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on simulating POVM measurements using a Bernoulli factory and reducing the quantum problem to a classical Gaussian testing problem.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the copy complexity scaling for purity estimation across different regimes of the error parameter $\varepsilon$, comparing non-adaptive and adaptive strategies.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first defining the problem and comparing it to the ideal case. It then develops and analyzes non-adaptive and adaptive estimators, providing upper bounds. Finally, it establishes lower bounds by relating the problem to classical Gaussian hypothesis testing, culminating in the optimal complexity characterization.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this work, we consider the fundamental task of estimating the purity of an unknown state to within $\textit{multiplicative}$ error $\varepsilon$. When one can perform general collective measurements, $Θ\left(\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon^2} + \frac{d}{\varepsilon}\right)$ copies are known to be necessary and sufficient for this problem [AISW20]. However, implementing collective measurements on such a large number of copies can be experimentally demanding, and we thus aim to characterize the copy complexity of this problem with incoherent measurements.   In this setting, the only non-trivial result is a non-adaptive algorithm that uses $O\left(   \frac{d}{\varepsilon^2} + \frac{d^2}{\varepsilon}   \right)$ copies [PTTW26], which is polynomially larger than the best-known lower bound. Our first result is a new algorithm performing non-adaptive incoherent measurements that succeeds using $O\left(   \frac{d}{\varepsilon^2} + \frac{d^{3/2}}{\varepsilon}   \right)$ copies, improving on the latter term in the copy complexity. Moreover, we show that for any algorithm restricted to non-adaptive measurements, the above copy complexity is optimal.   We also develop a new adaptive estimator for the purity of a state that improves on the above complexity in the high-precision regime, i.e., for $\varepsilon = o(1/d)$. We also show that the non-adaptive and adaptive estimators together yield the optimal complexity for incoherent purity estimation; in particular, we show that the copy complexity of this problem is $$   Θ\left(\min\left\{   \frac{d}{\varepsilon^2} + \frac{d^{3/2}}{\varepsilon}, \frac{d^2}{\varepsilon} + \frac{\sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon^2}\right\}   \right).   $$

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a novel quantum amplitude amplification protocol that enhances Grover's search by incorporating weak measurements within iterative loops. The methodology analyzes the expected oracle cost across regimes where the target probability is known, bounded, or completely unknown. The key finding is that this weak measurement approach provides provable oracle savings, maintaining the optimal $\Theta(1/\sqrt{p})$ scaling while offering explicit control mechanisms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, mathematically rigorous improvement to quantum search algorithms by integrating weak measurement feedback, which is highly relevant for understanding realistic quantum computation protocols subject to noise or incomplete knowledge.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop quantum amplitude amplification algorithms that improve upon standard Grover search by incorporating tunable weak measurements in iterative loops.

**Main result.** The proposed weakly measured loop achieves an expected oracle cost that improves upon standard Grover search, showing a leading constant of $1/\sqrt{2}$ in certain regimes and providing explicit fixed-point control.

**Method.** The authors analyze the expected oracle cost by modeling the process as an interleaving of ordinary Grover rotations and weak measurements, solving resulting differential/difference equations in various parameter regimes.

**Model / system.** The model is quantum amplitude amplification operating in a two-dimensional subspace, utilizing weak measurements defined by tunable strength $\kappa$ to probe the target subspace.

**Key observables.** Expected oracle cost (expected number of Grover iterations), which is analyzed in terms of the target probability $p$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Target probability $p$, weak measurement strength $\kappa$, and the lower bound $p_0$ for the target probability.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the process retains the Grover-type quadratic speedup and relies on bounding omitted tail sums for rigorous proofs.

**Figures summary.** Figure 2 plots the normalized expected cost $2C(b)/\pi$ vs. $b$, showing a minimum near $b \approx 5.2$. Figure 3 compares the finite-$p$ normalized expected cost for various adaptive schedules, highlighting the authors' schedule's performance.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the expected cost in three regimes: known $p$, lower-bounded $p \ge p_0$, and completely unknown $p$, progressing from exact solutions to adaptive, asymptotic analyses using Gamma functions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present a family of quantum amplitude amplification algorithms that interleave ordinary Grover rotations with tunable weak measurements in loops. A successful measurement yields the target state and stops the algorithm, while after a failure, the loop resumes from the post-measurement state without restarting. We express the leading costs in expected Grover iterations as $p \to 0$. For a known target probability $p$, an exact weak measurement-conditioned loop for states near the angle $π/4$ uses $(π/8+1/4+o(1))/\sqrt{p}$ iterations, improving on the standard Grover constant $π/4$ and on optimised restart Grover, and matching the corresponding infimum in our continuous-angle analysis. When only a lower bound $0 < p_0 \leq p < 1/2$ is available, a discrete Lyapunov equation gives the exact expected oracle cost for every fixed measurement strength and a closed-form optimal strength. Using the strength selected from $p_0$, the expected number of Grover iterations is at most $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{p_0}})$, where the expected cost decreases as the actual $p$ increases, and gives the leading constant $1/\sqrt{2}$ at the promise boundary $p = p_0$. For completely unknown $p$, we identify measurement strength $κ(t)=Θ(1/t)$ as the critical scale within the regular schedules considered here and analyse $κ_b(t)=\min\{1/2,b/t\}$. For each fixed $b > 2$, we rigorously derive a closed-form Gamma-function expression $C(b)$ giving $(C(b)/2+o(1))/\sqrt{p}$ expected iterations. Numerical minimisation of this explicit expression gives $b \approx 5.2$ and $C(b)/2 \approx 1.01$. The results show that weak measurements preserve the $Θ(1/\sqrt{p})$ search scale while adding an explicit fixed-point control mechanism and provable oracle savings.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a normal-ordered perturbative expansion method to calculate how a matter system evolves when coupled to a quantum light field. This technique is superior to conventional methods because it converges much faster at strong coupling strengths and correctly accounts for quantum effects missed by simpler approximations. It provides a robust theoretical framework for modeling light-matter interactions in quantum regimes.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, systematic, and highly convergent theoretical tool for analyzing open quantum systems where the coupling to a quantum bath (like the vacuum or a cavity field) is strong, which is central to quantum optics and cavity QED.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper develops a specialized perturbative expansion to accurately compute the reduced dynamics of a matter system coupled to a continuous-mode quantum photon field.

**Main result.** The normal-ordered expansion converges significantly faster than conventional methods, extending applicability to larger coupling strengths, and it provides an exact description for specific input states like $m$-photon Fock states.

**Method.** The core method is deriving a normal-ordered perturbative expansion for the reduced density matrix, which automatically handles field correlation functions and yields a master equation consistent with known quantum dynamics.

**Model / system.** The system models a general matter system coupled to a continuous-mode quantum photon field via a dipole-electric field interaction. The dynamics are governed by the total Hamiltonian, and the goal is to find the time evolution of the reduced system density matrix, $\rho_{sys}(t)$.

**Key observables.** The reduced system density matrix $\rho_{sys}(t)$, and the spontaneous emission term derived from the expansion.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The light-matter coupling strength, and the input photon state (e.g., coherent state, $m$-photon Fock state, cat state).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation assumes the initial total state is a product state, and the method is designed to overcome the limitations of the conventional expansion at strong coupling.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate Feynman diagrams representing the pathways contributing to the perturbative expansion at 2nd, 4th, and 6th orders, detailing the structure of the interaction superoperators.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the need for a normal-ordered approach, deriving the general form of the expansion, and then systematically calculating the contributions to the master equation order-by-order, comparing the results to known exact master equations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop a normal-ordered perturbative expansion method to compute the reduced dynamics of a matter system interacting with a general continuous-mode photon field state. In this expansion, all field correlation functions are automatically normal-ordered, while the free evolution is modified by spontaneous emission. Our normal-ordered expansion elucidates the physical meaning of non-normal-ordered correlation terms in the conventional expansion. Furthermore, under intermediate coupling strengths, the normal-ordered expansion converges significantly faster than the conventional expansion, allowing one to extend the applicability of perturbative expansion to much larger matter-light coupling strengths. Interestingly, given an $m$-photon Fock state input, the normal-ordered expansion truncates exactly at the $2m$-th order. For special classes of input states, we show the normal-ordered expansion is consistent with the corresponding master equations. We demonstrate the normal-ordered expansion numerically for a two-level system interacting with coherent state, $m$-photon Fock state, and cat state inputs.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a novel, single-contact quantum cooling mechanism to prepare a system's ground state from any mixed state. It achieves this by coherently transferring entropy into a bath that is only discarded at the end, avoiding the need for repeated resets. The protocol is rigorously proven for gapped fermionic systems and operates in polylogarithmic time.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a highly controlled, non-Markovian framework for quantum state preparation, which is crucial for implementing quantum simulations or quantum computation protocols where state purity is paramount.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of cooling an arbitrary mixed quantum state to its pure ground state by transferring entropy to an environment (bath) without requiring repeated bath resets.

**Main result.** A novel, single-contact, non-Markovian cooling protocol is rigorously developed that achieves ground-state preparation in polylogarithmic physical time relative to system size and desired accuracy.

**Method.** The method involves designing a time-dependent, coherent system-bath coupling Hamiltonian that guides the system through three controlled stages: Entrance, Transport, and Exit.

**Model / system.** The analysis is applied to weakly interacting, gapped fermionic systems on a lattice, modeled by a system Hamiltonian $H_u$ coupled to an environment bath via $H_{SE}(t)$.

**Key observables.** The primary observable is the fidelity of the final state $ho_{out}$ to the true ground state $|Gangle$, quantified by the trace-norm error $\epsilon$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The time scale $	au$ scales polylogarithmically with $N/\epsilon$, and the control strength must be parametrically larger than the local energy scale $\Lambda$ of the system.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The system Hamiltonian must be geometrically local and gapped, and the analysis relies on bounding errors across multiple sequential, controlled evolution stages.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 compares previous multi-round cooling protocols with the proposed single continuous joint evolution. Figure 2 illustrates the three-stage control path (Entrance, Transport, Exit) governing the time-dependent coupling.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the protocol by defining the total Hamiltonian, detailing the three sequential control stages (Entrance, Transport, Exit) required for the evolution, and finally providing rigorous mathematical bounds on the accumulated leakage and error across these stages.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Cooling an arbitrary mixed state to a pure ground state requires transferring its entropy to an environment. Can a single coherent bath contact accomplish this without repeated bath resets? We develop a new cooling mechanism that transfers the input information into bath degrees of freedom that subsequently decouple, while the system and the remaining bath follow a ground-state path. The bath is discarded only at the end, and the system Hamiltonian remains on and unmodified throughout. We rigorously realize this mechanism for a class of weakly interacting, gapped fermionic systems with local interactions. Starting from any mixed state, our protocol prepares the interacting ground state in total physical time polylogarithmic in the system size and inverse global trace-norm error. It uses two initially empty bath modes per system mode and a single pulse shared across all onsite system--bath couplings. The same pulse prepares each admissible system's own ground state without knowledge of its microscopic parameters. The guarantees follow directly from a non-Markovian system--bath dynamics without an effective Lindbladian description.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper models a quantum battery charging process by coupling a qubit to a thermal bath. It calculates the extractable work, or ergotropy, finding that this work plateaus at low temperatures, a behavior linked to the third law of thermodynamics. The study provides analytical insights into how coherence drives energy extraction in non-equilibrium steady states.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work connects non-equilibrium thermodynamics (ergotropy, steady states) directly to fundamental laws like the third law, using a controllable quantum system model (qubit battery) that is relevant to open quantum systems research.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the ergotropy and thermodynamic potentials of a qubit battery charged by thermal interactions, focusing on the role of energetic coherence and the third law of thermodynamics.

**Main result.** The ergotropy exhibits a plateau at low temperatures, which is traced to the third law of thermodynamics, showing proportionality to the equilibrium enthalpy. The charged state is a non-equilibrium steady state sustained by work.

**Method.** The analysis uses a quantum collision model framework, solving the Lindblad master equation to find steady-state expectation values for coherence and ergotropy.

**Model / system.** The system is a qubit battery (two-level system) coupled to a bath composed of clusters of ancillas (qubits or oscillators) via a composite interaction Hamiltonian. The dynamics are described by a Lindblad master equation.

**Key observables.** Ergotropy (W), Steady-State Coherence (SSC), Internal Energy (U), and the work cost required for charging.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Bath statistics parameter (lambda), temperature (T), and cluster size (N). The large-cluster limit (N >> 1) is a key regime.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes weak-coupling dynamics leading to a Markovian limit, and that the bath is in a Gibbs state.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the steady-state ergotropy vs. temperature, showing the low-T plateau, and compare the scaling of coherence (exponential) versus ergotropy (linear) with system size.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the dynamics using a master equation, calculates steady-state coherence and ergotropy in closed form for finite and large clusters, and analyzes the temperature dependence and thermodynamic implications, particularly linking the low-T plateau to the third law.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the ergotropy and the thermodynamic potentials of a qubit battery charged by repeated interactions with clusters of thermal ancillas, qubits or oscillators, through a composite system-bath coupling that generates steady-state coherence in the energy basis. A single parameter encoding the bath quantum statistics yields the coherence and ergotropy in closed form for any cluster size. For large clusters, the ergotropy becomes independent of the bath statistics and, at optimal couplings, reaches a universal fraction of the equilibrium internal energy of the qubit at the bath temperature. Since the charged state has no population inversion, all extractable work comes from coherence. The ergotropy is flat at low temperatures. We trace this plateau to the third law, and show that the ergotropy is proportional to the equilibrium enthalpy of the qubit, whose slope vanishes with the heat capacity. For a battery composed of multiple qubits, the coherence grows exponentially with the number of qubits while the ergotropy grows linearly, both remaining a nearly constant fraction of their respective maxima. The charged state is a non-equilibrium steady state with finite entropy at zero temperature, sustained by the work of switching the collisional interaction on and off. The cost is nonzero whenever the parallel coupling is nonzero, and, unlike the ergotropy, it depends on the bath statistics.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper numerically models frequency comb generation in an active optomechanical cavity formed by a VCSEL coupled to a MEMS mirror. By analyzing the coupled dynamics, the authors demonstrate that the resulting optical spectrum is a comb whose detailed structure is governed by the mechanical damping, resonance frequencies, and initial excitation levels. This work is significant for understanding controlled, nonlinear light sources in integrated quantum optics platforms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses nonlinear cavity dynamics and optomechanical coupling, which are central themes in cavity QED and open quantum systems. The detailed mapping of spectral features to mechanical parameters provides a rich platform for understanding quantum light sources.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the generation of optical frequency combs in an active optomechanical cavity system.

**Main result.** The system self-sustainably generates a frequency comb whose structure is highly dependent on mechanical dissipation, resonance frequencies, and initial excitation amplitudes.

**Method.** The study uses numerical simulations to solve coupled rate equations describing mechanical motion, carrier density, and photon density.

**Model / system.** The physical system is an electrically pumped VCSEL coupled to two mechanical modes of a suspended MEMS mirror. The dynamics are modeled by coupling the mechanical oscillators to the cavity photon and carrier dynamics via radiation-pressure feedback.

**Key observables.** Frequency-comb structure in the photon-density spectrum, threshold current ($I_{th}$), and relative spectral intensities of comb lines.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Mechanical quality factors ($Q_j$), mechanical resonance frequencies ($f_j$), and initial mechanical amplitudes ($A_j(0)$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model neglects direct elastic and photothermal coupling, and the calculated spectrum is for the intracavity intensity variable, requiring phase-resolved calculation for full field coherence.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the device structure, the time and spectrum of the comb in photon density, and the dependence of the comb structure and threshold current on varying quality factors, resonance frequencies, and initial amplitudes.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the coupled dynamical model, analyzes the spectral components arising from nonlinear cavity response, and systematically investigates how varying mechanical parameters (dissipation, frequency, initial amplitude) controls the resulting comb structure and the system's operating threshold.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We numerically investigate frequency-comb generation in an electrically pumped vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser coupled to two mechanical modes of a suspended mirror. Displacement-dependent cavity loss and radiation-pressure feedback couple the mechanical motion to the carrier and photon densities, producing harmonics and combination-frequency components in the photon-density spectrum. Mechanical quality factors primarily control the intensity of comb lines, whereas resonance frequencies determine their spectral distribution. The initial mechanical amplitudes influence the threshold current and relative spectral intensities, with the simultaneous excitation of both modes yielding a broader set of observable components. These results establish the dependence of the calculated comb structure on mechanical dissipation, resonance frequencies, and initial conditions in an active optomechanical cavity.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a theoretical framework for phase separation in exotic 'fractonic fluids' characterized by conserved higher-order multipole moments. It rigorously compares equilibrium and non-equilibrium dynamics, demonstrating that these conservation laws significantly slow down relaxation processes. The findings highlight how non-equilibrium conditions can suppress fluctuations and alter the dynamics of phase separation.

**Why it may be interesting.** The explicit comparison between equilibrium and non-equilibrium dynamics, particularly the role of FDT violations, provides a rich theoretical framework applicable to non-equilibrium many-body systems, which is relevant to open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper develops a theory for phase separation in 'fractonic fluids'—fluids conserving higher-order multipole moments—and investigates how these constraints modify coarsening, nucleation, and fluctuation dynamics.

**Main result.** Higher-order conservation laws are shown to slow down relaxation processes, while non-equilibrium violations of the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem suppress fluctuations and hinder nucleation.

**Method.** The analysis uses a coarse-grained hydrodynamic field theory, comparing equilibrium and non-equilibrium dynamics by analyzing the structure factor and relaxation times.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled as a fluid described by a scalar density $\rho$ exhibiting 'fractonic behavior' due to higher-order multipole conservation laws. The dynamics are governed by a generalized hydrodynamic equation incorporating noise and deterministic relaxation terms.

**Key observables.** Structure factor $S(k, t)$, relaxation time $\tau_k$, characteristic domain size $L_S(t)$, and the activation barrier $\Delta V_c$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The order of multipole conservation ($P$), the Laplacian power ($m$), and the dimensionality ($d$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The theory assumes a local gradient expansion for the stationary measure, and specific scaling assumptions are made in the marginal case ($d=2$) for barrier calculations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate relaxation times and stationary structure factors for various conservation orders, and show domain size growth during phase separation, comparing equilibrium and non-equilibrium dynamics.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the hydrodynamic theory, analyzes the comparison between equilibrium (FDT-constrained) and non-equilibrium dynamics, derives scaling laws for relaxation times and activation barriers, and discusses the implications for hyperuniformity.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop a theory of phase separation in fluids conserving higher-order multipole moments of a scalar density, and investigate the resulting coarsening dynamics, nucleation, and interfacial fluctuations. We find that higher-order conservation laws slow the relaxation of all phenomena investigated, whereas nonequilibrium violations of the fluctuation--dissipation theorem suppress density and interfacial fluctuations while hindering nucleation. Simulations support these predictions.

**Summary.** This paper proposes a novel platform for matter-wave interferometry by embedding rare-earth ions within microparticles. It theoretically addresses the major hurdle of decoherence by showing that increasing the particle mass can suppress environmental decoherence rates. The result establishes a pathway for building quantum sensors capable of testing fundamental physics with unprecedented sensitivity.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it merges quantum optics, solid-state physics, and quantum sensing. The detailed analysis of decoherence scaling with mass and the use of embedded quantum emitters (rare-earth ions) in solid-state hosts provide a concrete, advanced platform for studying open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is developing matter-wave interferometry using large, massive particles to enable precise tests of fundamental physics, which is severely limited by decoherence.

**Main result.** The proposal demonstrates that using rare-earth ions in microparticles, combined with specific interferometer geometries, allows decoherence rates to decrease or remain constant as particle mass increases, enabling high-precision sensing.

**Method.** The work combines theoretical analysis of decoherence mechanisms (from background gas and blackbody radiation) with a proposed experimental setup utilizing optical Raman transitions on embedded rare-earth ions.

**Model / system.** The system is a matter-wave interferometer using a microparticle doped with a rare-earth ion (e.g., Sm3+ in SrSe). The interference phase is read out via the quantum state of the ion, and decoherence is modeled by analyzing scattering interactions between the particle and the environment.

**Key observables.** Phase sensitivity ($\phi/g$), coherence time ($T$), decoherence rate ($\Gamma$), and the macroscopicity parameter ($\mu$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Microparticle mass ($m$), vacuum level (moderate vacuum), photon count ($\sim 10^3$), and the rare-earth ion's angular momentum state ($J=1/2$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Decoherence due to blackbody radiation is assumed negligible, and the analysis relies on specific limits for the ratio between path separation ($\Delta x$) and momentum exchange wavelength ($\lambda$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the Mach-Zehnder interferometer sequence using Raman transitions and show the calculated decoherence rate due to optical photon scattering as a function of microparticle mass.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the need for high-mass interferometry, then details the physical system using rare-earth ions and optical transitions. It proceeds to analyze decoherence from various sources (gas, BBR, optical), deriving theoretical models for the rate dependence on mass and path separation.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Matter-wave interferometers are sensitive probes of low energy physics and have been used for precise tests of gravity and quantum mechanics. These applications would benefit from interfering particles of higher mass, but observing the interference of a large particle is challenging due to the need to control its initial state and to avoid decoherence. Here we propose to demonstrate matter-wave interference of a microparticle with an embedded rare-earth ion. Optical transitions of the rare-earth ion will impart momentum to the microparticle's center of mass. The use of a time-symmetric interferometer geometry and a rare-earth ion state with angular momentum $J = 1/2$ will eliminate sensitivity to the initial conditions of the microparticle. We show that the rates of all relevant external decoherence mechanisms either decrease or remain constant as the microparticle mass is increased, allowing decoherence to be avoided by using sufficiently large particles. An apparatus at moderate vacuum levels will support microparticle interferometry with up to $10^3$ photons per beam splitter and millisecond coherence time. This demonstration will establish microparticle interferometry as a new platform for quantum sensing, improving searches for minimal modifications of quantum mechanics by up to four orders of magnitude in the near term and laying the foundation for future gravitational tests.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a novel 'pseudo-control protocol' to estimate the memory dimension of open quantum dynamics. By analyzing the rank of an interference matrix derived from two sequential system-environment interactions, the authors establish a lower bound on the environmental memory. This technique allows for the characterization of complex system-environment interactions in many-body quantum systems without requiring full environmental tomography.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, experimentally accessible diagnostic tool for characterizing complex, non-Markovian environmental coupling in quantum systems, which is crucial for understanding decoherence mechanisms in quantum computation and simulation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to characterize the memory dimension of open quantum dynamics, which quantifies the essential environmental resources shaping system evolution.

**Main result.** A pseudo-control protocol was developed that uses the rank of an interference matrix to establish a lower bound on the memory dimension without full process tomography.

**Method.** The protocol involves comparing the system's evolution under two separate interactions separated by a waiting time, generating an interference matrix whose rank is analyzed.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on open quantum dynamics involving a system (S) coupled to an environment (E), modeled using Lindblad-type master equations for the evolution during interaction and waiting periods.

**Key observables.** The primary observable is the 'resolved rank' ($r_\epsilon$) of the interference matrix (MRS), which provides a lower bound on the memory dimension ($d_m \ge \lceil\sqrt{r_\epsilon}ceil$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Interaction time ($	au$), interval time ($T$), coupling strength ($\lambda$), and the specific coupling geometry (boundary vs. ladder).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The bound derived from the rank is one-sided (high rank $\implies$ large memory, but low rank $
ot\implies$ little memory). The analysis relies on a fixed resolution scale ($\epsilon$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the temporal dependence of the resolved rank ($r_\epsilon$) for various environmental models (A-E) under changes in $	au$ and $T$, and compare the spectral evolution between dissipative (Model C) and coherent (Model E) environments.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the memory dimension concept, details the pseudo-control protocol and the resulting rank bound, and then applies this method to test various quantum many-body models (Ising, XXZ) under different environmental coupling geometries and time scales.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Characterising open quantum dynamics requires identifying the environmental degrees of freedom that shape the system's evolution. The memory dimension, defined as the size of the smallest effective memory needed to reproduce this influence, quantifies the dynamically relevant environmental resources and provides a common basis for comparing different many-body environments. Here we introduce a pseudo-control protocol that encodes information about the memory dimension in an experimentally accessible interference matrix, whose rank certifies a lower bound on this dimension without direct access to the environment or full process-tensor tomography. Applied to quantum many-body environments, the protocol allows flexible adjustment of the interaction and interval times, revealing how these parameters, environmental dynamics, and system-environment interactions shape detectable memory. Our approach provides a new operational technique for characterising open quantum dynamics and probing the structure of system-environment interactions through their memory signatures.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a comprehensive theory to optimally place absorbing traps in heterogeneous media to minimize particle capture time. It identifies distinct scaling laws for the optimal trap density based on whether the trapping is weak or strong. The key finding is that setting the initial particle distribution to the equilibrium distribution yields a constant, minimized MFPT regardless of trapping strength.

**Why it may be interesting.** The mathematical framework for optimizing absorption rates in heterogeneous media is highly relevant to open quantum systems, particularly in understanding decoherence or engineered dissipation channels where trapping/loss mechanisms are crucial.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the optimal placement of numerous small absorbing traps to minimize the mean first-passage time (MFPT) for diffusing particles in a medium with spatially varying diffusivity.

**Main result.** The optimal trap density $ho(x)$ depends on the trapping strength regime, yielding arithmetic averaging ($ho \propto \mu + \omega$) in the weak regime and geometric averaging ($ho \propto \sqrt{\mu\omega}$) in the strong regime.

**Method.** The authors develop a homogenization approach to unify the analysis across different trapping strengths, complementing the classical Green's function method.

**Model / system.** The system models particle diffusion governed by the Fokker-Planck equation in a heterogeneous domain $\Omega$, characterized by a space-dependent diffusivity $D(x)$. The optimization seeks to minimize the MFPT by controlling the trap density $ho(x)$.

**Key observables.** Mean First-Passage Time (MFPT), optimal trap density $ho(x)$, and the worst-case capture time.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Trapping strength ($\kappa$), initial particle distribution ($\omega(x)$), and the equilibrium distribution ($\mu(x) \propto 1/D(x)$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on asymptotic methods, including the weak trapping limit ($\kappa \ll 1$) and the homogenization approach, which assumes a dilute trap ensemble.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare numerical results (e.g., Voronoi diagrams) of the optimal trap distribution $ho(x)$ against the theoretical continuum limit predictions.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the physical problem and the governing equations, then deriving optimal density formulas for weak and strong trapping regimes, developing the general homogenization approach, and finally analyzing special cases like $\omega = \mu$ and 1D/2D scaling laws.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the problem of optimally placing a large number of small absorbing traps to minimize the mean first-passage time (MFPT) of particles diffusing in a heterogeneous medium with space-dependent diffusivity $D(x)$ and prescribed initial particle distribution $ω(x)$. In two and three dimensions we identify two distinct regimes, depending on how strongly the trap ensemble depletes the particles. In the weak trapping regime (fewer traps) the optimal trap density $ρ$ is the arithmetic average $ρ= \frac12(μ+ω)$ of the normalized inverse diffusivity $μ\propto 1/D$ and the initial particle distribution $ω$. In the strong trapping regime (more traps), it is proportional to their geometric average, $ρ\propto \sqrt{μω}$. We revisit the classical Green's function approach and show that it applies to weak trapping only; in 2D this requires the trap size to be exponentially small in the number of traps, so that most applications of interest fall in the strong trapping regime instead. We therefore develop a homogenization approach that captures both regimes. A special choice of initial particle distribution is $ω\propto 1/D$, which corresponds to the equilibrium particle distribution in the absence of traps according to the Itô interpretation. In this case we show that the optimal trap distribution is the stationary particle distribution itself, regardless of the trapping strength, and this makes the MFPT constant throughout the domain; the same trap distribution also minimizes the worst-case capture time. Finally, in one dimension we find instead $ρ\propto\left(μω\right) ^{1/3}$, and a similar analysis covers space-dependent drift and thin domains of variable cross-section. Direct numerical optimization confirms the analytical results.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a theory for Quantum Reservoir Computing by replacing standard Markovian dissipation with non-Markovian dynamics modeled via fractional calculus. The authors demonstrate that this non-Markovian memory acts as a computational resource, boosting short-term memory and prediction accuracy. This highlights that system-environment interaction can actively encode useful memory into the quantum evolution.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a concrete theoretical framework showing how engineered dissipation (non-Markovianity) can be harnessed not just as a source of decoherence, but as a tunable resource to enhance specific computational capabilities in quantum information processing.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the computational potential of non-Markovian memory effects in Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC), moving beyond the standard Markovian assumption.

**Main result.** Non-Markovian dissipation acts as an active resource, significantly enhancing short-term linear and non-linear memory capacity, although this comes at the cost of long-range temporal retention.

**Method.** The authors model the dynamics using a fractional derivative (Caputo derivative) approach, which mathematically implements non-Markovian time subordination.

**Model / system.** The system is a one-dimensional spin-1/2 chain acting as the reservoir, governed by a Hamiltonian and subjected to dissipation modeled by fractional derivatives.

**Key observables.** Short-Term Memory (STM) capacity ($MC_	au$), Normalized Mean Square Error (NMSE) for NARMA-p tasks, and non-Markovianity quantified by the BLP measure.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The fractional order $\alpha \in (0, 1]$ controls the degree of non-Markovianity; the time delay $\tau$ dictates the memory regime.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The use of the Caputo fractional derivative is employed for physical consistency, and the analysis relies on the reservoir mapping inputs into a high-dimensional feature space.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the QRC architecture comparing Markovian ($\alpha=1$) and non-Markovian ($\alpha<1$) dissipation, and show quantitative results for memory capacity and prediction error vs. $\alpha$ and task order $p$.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the QRC framework, generalizes the dynamics using fractional derivatives, analyzes memory retention using diagnostics like STM capacity and BLP measure, and finally benchmarks performance on non-linear tasks like NARMA-p.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The control of open-system dynamics provides a powerful mechanism for using quantum information to process sequential tasks. While quantum reservoir computing typically relies on Markovian dissipation to process sequential data, the computational role of non-Markovian memory effects remains largely unexplored. We introduce a framework for quantum reservoir computing where non-Markovianity is explicitly modeled and regulated using fractional derivatives. By employing fractional time subordination, we generate tunable, heavy-tailed relaxation dynamics that govern the information backflow between the system and its environment. Non-Markovian information backflow regulates the overall temporal retention of the system, maximizing short-term linear memory capacity. Within an optimal operating regime, fractional non-Markovianity redistributes the reservoir memory towards recent inputs, improving both linear memory capacity and nonlinear prediction accuracy at short delays, at the expense of long-range temporal retention. System-environment interaction proves being not merely a requirement for quantum reservoir computing, but an active resource that embeds memory retention directly into the quantum evolution.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a rigorous stochastic framework to study opinion dynamics when subjected to sudden, large-scale exogenous shocks. By coupling local interaction rules (like the voter model) with external forcing, the authors show that these shocks can fundamentally change the system's behavior, leading to complex phase diagrams and allowing for the calculation of optimal shock rates to accelerate or delay consensus.

**Why it may be interesting.** The framework of incorporating external, non-local forcing into standard interacting particle systems (like the voter model) is highly relevant to understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in complex systems, which shares mathematical structure with open quantum systems driven by external fields.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how large-scale, sudden exogenous shocks affect the collective opinion dynamics of a population, which standard local-interaction models fail to capture.

**Main result.** Shocks can significantly alter consensus formation, leading to rich phase diagrams that exhibit novel trimodal or asymmetric bimodal states, and the optimal shock rate can be identified to minimize the time to consensus.

**Method.** The dynamics are modeled using a composite stochastic process, combining the baseline local interaction (e.g., voter model) with an exogenous jump term, analyzed via master equations and Laplace transforms.

**Model / system.** The system models opinion dynamics using agents with binary opinions ($\{-1, 1\}$) interacting on a network. The dynamics are governed by a composite transition matrix $P_r = (1-r)P + rR$, where $P$ is the local process and $R$ encodes the shock effect.

**Key observables.** Global magnetization ($m$), Mean First-Passage Time (MFPT) to consensus, and the steady-state probability density function (PDF) of magnetization.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Shock probability ($r$), initial magnetization ($m_0$), and the structure of the exogenous shock distribution ($\psi(m_r)$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The shock effect can be incorporated linearly into the transition matrix, and the analysis often relies on approximations like the renewal theory or Laplace transforms for tractability.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the macroscopic shifting dynamics (random walk interrupted by jumps), the dependence of MFPT on initial magnetization and shock rate, and the comparison of analytical vs. Monte Carlo results for the FPT distribution.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds a general stochastic framework for composite dynamics, applies it to the voter model, derives analytical tools (like the Laplace transform for FPT), and analyzes specific regimes (e.g., all-to-all noisy voter model) to characterize the resulting phase diagrams.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Large-scale events such as political scandals or misinformation campaigns can abruptly shift the collective opinion of a population and reshape the dynamics in ways that standard local-interaction models of sociophysics do not capture. Here, we investigate the dynamics of opinion formation when a group of interacting agents is subjected to sudden, macroscopic exogenous shocks. Our framework is general and applies to arbitrary opinion dynamics models; to illustrate its scope, we consider the voter model and variations thereof. We verify that the mathematical description is excellent in describing the first-passage properties to consensus of the voter model on the complete graph and on complex networks. Remarkably, we identify the conditions under which shocks can be advantageous or detrimental to reach consensus. For the case of the all-to-all noisy voter model under exogenous events, we unveil a rich phase diagram characterized by novel trimodal and asymmetric bimodal states. Ultimately, this work provides a rigorous yet flexible stochastic-process framework for understanding the out-of-equilibrium behavior of opinion dynamics under recurrent exogenous stressors.

</details>
