**Summary.** This paper analyzes a three-level quantum heat engine, showing that parasitic heat leaks degrade performance by creating a thermodynamic short circuit. By modeling the system with a physical spectral filter, the authors demonstrate that while spectral selectivity is beneficial, narrowing the filter too much incurs a cost in the engine's achievable power output.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the practical limitations of quantum thermal machines by quantifying the unavoidable trade-off between spectral purity (selectivity) and operational speed (throughput) imposed by real-world filters.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how finite-bandwidth reservoir engineering can protect a three-level quantum heat engine from parasitic heat leaks that degrade performance.

**Main result.** Spectral selectivity can protect the useful thermodynamic cycle, but a real physical filter cannot be narrowed indefinitely without incurring a measurable dynamical throughput cost.

**Method.** The authors compare results from multiple open-system descriptions, including the local GKSL master equation and the nonsecular Bloch–Redfield treatment, to analyze the system dynamics.

**Model / system.** The system is a continuous three-level quantum heat engine modeled with useful and parasitic couplings, and the filtering mechanism is introduced via an explicit damped auxiliary harmonic mode.

**Key observables.** Efficiency ($\eta$), stationary output power ($P$), and the maximum-power bandwidth ($\kappa_\star$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Filter linewidth ($\kappa$), coupling strengths ($g_h, g_\ell$), and temperature ratios ($T_h/T_c$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis compares results from different theoretical approximations (GKSL vs. Redfield) and notes the limitations of the fully secular global model in the weak-coupling limit.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the engine cycle, comparing the useful hot transition against the parasitic coupling, and show the dependence of maximum power on the filter linewidth ($\kappa$).

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the ideal rate network, then introduces the physical filter via an auxiliary mode, and finally compares the predictions of the GKSL, Redfield, and rate-only models to derive the final design principle.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Finite-bandwidth reservoir engineering can suppress unwanted transitions in a quantum thermal machine, but a physical filter also introduces a finite response time. We study this competition in a continuous three-level heat engine whose hot environment couples parasitically to the cold transition. The corresponding three-state rate network is solved exactly, showing that the parasitic transition produces a hot-to-cold thermodynamic short circuit and yielding a closed threshold for the loss of positive-power operation. We then retain a damped auxiliary mode explicitly as a physical spectral filter. Its Lorentzian response suppresses the detuned parasitic transition, whereas excessive narrowing limits the useful energy throughput. Independent local-GKSL and nonsecular Bloch--Redfield calculations both recover the no-leak Markovian engine in the weak-coupling limit and predict a finite maximum-power bandwidth, although its precise location is model dependent. A frequency-resolved Lorentzian-rate reduction, by contrast, has no interior optimum. The resulting design principle is that spectral selectivity can protect the useful thermodynamic cycle, but a real filter cannot be narrowed without a dynamical throughput cost.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper establishes fundamental bounds on how much quantum interference information can be recovered when only local measurements or controls are available. By analyzing critical quantum spin chains, the authors prove that the inherent critical orthogonality exponent remains invariant under optimal local recovery protocols. This work sets rigorous limits on the information extractable from a system when global control is impossible.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides deep insights into the robustness of critical quantum phenomena against local perturbations, which is crucial for understanding quantum error correction and the limits of measurement in complex quantum many-body systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the fundamental limit of interference recovery (quantum erasure) when only local control is available over a quantum system, specifically determining if optimal local recovery can alter critical orthogonality exponents.

**Main result.** The authors prove that optimal local recovery cannot alter the critical orthogonality exponent, demonstrating that this exponent governs the collective limit of interference loss even when local control is applied.

**Method.** The analysis employs rigorous mathematical bounds, including local amplitude-ratio bounds, comparison of full vs. recovered fidelity ($F_{	ext{full}}$ vs $F_R$), and techniques involving imaginary-time evolution and Cauchy product asymptotics.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on quantum spin environments, exemplified by a connected critical Ising chain. The system is described by Hamiltonians involving local bias terms and is analyzed in the context of finite-region erasure.

**Key observables.** Orthogonality exponent, fidelity ($F_{	ext{full}}$, $F_R$), recovery gain ($\Lambda_M$), and local component ratios.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The critical exponent (e.g., $1/8$ for the Ising chain), the size of the controlled region ($|M|$), and local energy scales ($\Lambda_M$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes positive ground-state Hamiltonians and uniformly bounded ratios of local longitudinal bias to transverse field, and requires no gap in the environment.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 compares the bare overlap and optimized amplitude for a sign-defect chain, showing the preservation of the critical exponent. Figure 2 illustrates recoverable local records at finite mediator energy.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops bounds by comparing full state overlaps to locally recovered states, deriving local amplitude-ratio bounds, and applying these to specific models like the Ising chain to prove the invariance of critical exponents.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We prove a local amplitude-ratio bound for positive ground states and an explicit reverse comparison for fidelity under finite-region erasure. An exact lattice calculation for a connected critical Ising chain gives amplitude exponent $1/8$, preserved by arbitrary optimal control on any fixed spin set and, at the level of logarithmic exponents, on $o(\log N)$ spins. We derive the finite Cauchy product and its uniform strip asymptotics, and document exact two-spin optimization and an interferometric protocol for measuring the recovery. A separate finite-mediator theorem quantifies local compression and a decoder while retaining the rest of the environment exactly. We also give a ground-preparation Ramsey bound, counterexamples to stronger projected-state inferences, and independent full-Hamiltonian calculations.

</details>

**Summary.** This work establishes a spectral theory for calculating large deviations in complex, non-Markovian systems. By using a WKBJ Ansatz on the Feynman-Kac equation, the authors transform the problem into an eigenvalue problem governed by Hamilton-Jacobi characteristics. This provides a powerful, efficient tool for quantifying rare fluctuations in systems with memory effects, such as self-interacting jump processes.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous mathematical machinery developed—linking spectral theory, WKBJ methods, and Hamilton-Jacobi dynamics—is highly relevant for analyzing non-equilibrium dynamics in open quantum systems where memory effects are crucial.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper develops a spectral theory to analyze dynamical large deviations in complex, non-Markovian, self-interacting processes.

**Main result.** The problem is successfully recast as an eigenvalue problem for a tilted operator coupled to Hamilton-Jacobi characteristics, providing a computationally efficient framework for quantifying fluctuations.

**Method.** The authors employ a multiscale Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin-Jeffreys (WKBJ) Ansatz to solve the Feynman-Kac equation, reducing the dynamics to solving characteristic equations derived from a Hamilton-Jacobi framework.

**Model / system.** The theory applies to non-Markov jump processes (SIJPs) and non-Markov chains (SIMCs) whose evolution depends on the system's history via empirical observables (memory). An example used is the bistable self-induced East model.

**Key observables.** Empirical measure ($L_x$), empirical flux ($\Phi_{xy}$), Scaled Cumulant Generating Function (SCGF), and the rate function $I^*$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The memory variable $a$ and its conjugate momentum $P$, which govern the slow evolution of the system.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method relies on the WKBJ approximation, which separates fast configurational relaxation from slow memory evolution, and assumes the existence of a compact interval $K$ for the memory variable.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1(a) compares the SCGF of the activity for the self-induced East model at various sizes ($N=6, 8, 10$) against the standard Markov East model.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds the theory by first deriving the Feynman-Kac equation for the MGF, then applying the WKBJ Ansatz to transform it into an eigenvalue problem. This is subsequently linked to a Hamilton-Jacobi equation, whose characteristics govern the slow memory evolution, culminating in the calculation of the rate function via the SCGF.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop a spectral theory for dynamical large deviations in non-Markov jump processes and non-Markov chains, whose dynamics depends on the past through state- and jump-dependent empirical observables. We demonstrate that a multiscale Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin-Jeffreys (WKBJ) Ansatz separates fast configurational relaxation from slow memory evolution, reducing the Feynman--Kac equation for occupation and flux statistics to an eigenvalue problem for a new tilted operator coupled to Hamilton--Jacobi characteristics. This provides a computationally efficient framework for quantifying fluctuations in a broad class of non-Markovian systems. We illustrate our general results with a bistable self-induced East model.

</details>

**Summary.** This work proposes a defect-aware parallel protocol to efficiently reload atoms into the defect sites of neutral-atom quantum computers. By combining coherent quantum operations with a fast, optimized planning algorithm, the authors demonstrate a substantial increase in atom filling rates. This research is crucial for realizing fault-tolerant, continuous quantum computation by addressing resource depletion.

**Why it may be interesting.** It directly tackles a major engineering bottleneck for scalable quantum computation—maintaining qubit connectivity and resource availability—by optimizing the physical resource management layer.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the critical need to maintain high atom filling rates in neutral-atom quantum computers by developing an efficient protocol to reload atoms into defect sites.

**Main result.** The proposed defect-aware protocol significantly improves the average atom filling rate (e.g., from 98.61% to 99.94% in low-noise conditions) while maintaining planning times fast enough for real-time operation.

**Method.** The method combines a coherent atom reloading operation, which preserves quantum information, with a defect-aware planner that determines the optimal atom reloading pattern.

**Model / system.** The system is a neutral-atom quantum computer utilizing a storage atom array and an entanglement atom array, connected by an optical tweezer array for atom transport.

**Key observables.** Average atom filling rate, planning time.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Array size (e.g., $36 	imes 90$), noise level (low/high).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The protocol assumes a low-noise environment for peak performance demonstration; the planner's performance is compared against an exact Mixed Integer Programming (MIP) solver.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 schematically illustrates the system model, showing the Storage Array, Entanglement Array, and Tweezer Array, defining occupied sites and defects.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this work, we propose a defect-aware parallel atom reloading protocol that reloads atoms based on defect information to increase the atom filling rate. The proposed protocol is useful for neutral-atom quantum computers, where reloading atoms into the defects, or atom-loss positions, is mandatory for continuous operation against atom loss. Our protocol takes advantage of both parallelism and defect awareness to improve atom-reloading efficiency. The proposed protocol consists of the coherent atom reloading operation and the defect-aware planner. The former replenishes the defects with atoms preserving the quantum information coherently. This coherence allows us to adaptively choose the reloading strategy based on the current defect configuration. The latter determines the atom reloading pattern to efficiently replenish the defects. In numerical experiments assuming a low-noise environment, we confirmed that the average atom filling rate improved from 98.61% to 99.94% for a 36 x 90 atom array, matching the filling rate obtained with a mixed integer programming solver to within 0.001 percentage points while planning each reload in under 0.1 ms. These results demonstrate that defect-aware parallel reloading can achieve and sustain high atom filling rates while the performance of the defect-aware planner meets the real-time requirements of neutral-atom quantum computers.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a locality-based framework to accelerate the simulation of time-accumulated observables (dense outputs) in quantum many-body systems. By leveraging Lieb-Robinson bounds, the authors demonstrate that restricting the simulation to a local region around the observable is sufficient to achieve high accuracy. This significantly reduces computational resource requirements, making simulations of large, complex lattice models more feasible.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a crucial theoretical tool for simulating large, complex quantum systems by proving that local information access is sufficient for calculating time-integrated observables, which is vital for simulating dynamics in condensed matter systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently estimating time-accumulated observables (dense outputs) in quantum simulations, which traditionally requires resources scaling with the full Hamiltonian norm.

**Main result.** By developing a locality-based truncation framework utilizing Lieb-Robinson bounds, the authors show that local simulation resources can recover the dense output, leading to query complexity that can be independent of the total system size.

**Method.** The core method involves spatially truncating the Hamiltonian to a local region and rigorously bounding the resulting error using Lieb-Robinson bounds, which are then translated into local-simulation query bounds.

**Model / system.** The analysis applies to quantum many-body systems on a lattice, covering free and interacting fermionic and bosonic models, as well as open quantum systems governed by Lindbladians.

**Key observables.** Dense Output: $\mathcal{J}_H(O) = \int_0^T \langle \psi(t)|O(t)|\psi(t)angle dt$; Local-simulation query bounds.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Evolution time $T$, target precision $\epsilon$, system size $N$, and the decay exponent $\alpha$ governing Hamiltonian locality.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the existence of spatial locality bounds (Lieb-Robinson bounds) and the ability to truncate the Hamiltonian while maintaining controlled error bounds.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the dependence of the required local region on simulation time and precision, and demonstrate the resource improvement by comparing local vs. full Hamiltonian norms.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem of dense output estimation, introduces the locality-based truncation framework using LRBs, provides theoretical bounds for various lattice systems (fermions/bosons/open systems), and concludes with numerical verification and complexity analysis.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Estimating time-accumulated observables, or dense outputs, is central to extracting classical information from quantum simulations. Whereas most quantum-simulation algorithms aim to reproduce a final state or a single-time expectation value, many applications require the integrated signal $J_H(O)=\int_0^T \langle ψ(t)|O(t)|ψ(t)\rangle\,dt$. Previous Hamiltonian-simulation-based dense-output algorithms have query costs that depend on the norm of the full Hamiltonian, which can grow with system size. However, one can naturally optimize the simulation algorithm when the system structure is known. Consequently, we develop a locality-based truncation framework for the dense-output problem on lattice Hamiltonians. By truncating the Hamiltonian and tightening the resulting error with Lieb-Robinson bounds, we show that a local simulation can recover the dense output. We bound the quantum simulation error from spatial truncation and translate it into local-simulation query bounds. Our analysis includes free and interacting systems for both fermions and bosons, as well as open quantum systems governed by Lindbladians. The improvement from our truncation algorithm varies from constant to unbounded as the system size grows. We also give example applications and conduct relevant numerical experiments to support our findings.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces CYNAR, a novel computational pipeline designed to estimate the entropy production rate ($\sigma$) from noisy, partially observed trajectories in non-equilibrium systems. It achieves this by decomposing $\sigma$ into a 'traffic' term derived from correlation function curvature and an 'inflow rate' from the steady-state score. CYNAR is shown to be significantly more robust and theoretically sound than existing methods, making it valuable for analyzing complex stochastic dynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous statistical framework for estimating non-equilibrium quantities like entropy production is crucial for understanding dissipation in open quantum systems and quantum thermodynamics, providing a powerful tool for analyzing measurement data.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is accurately inferring the entropy production rate ($\sigma$) from recorded system trajectories, especially when the underlying physical forces are unknown or only partial measurements are available.

**Main result.** The proposed CYNAR estimator provides a more reliable, unbiased, and robust method for estimating $\sigma$ compared to standard current-based approaches, particularly under partial observation.

**Method.** CYNAR estimates $\sigma$ using a kinetic decomposition: $\sigma = 4T + G$, where $T$ (Traffic) is derived from the short-time curvature of correlation functions, and $G$ (Inflow Rate) is computed from the steady-state score function.

**Model / system.** The analysis is based on overdamped stochastic differential equations ($\dot{x}_t = a(x_t) + \sqrt{2D} \xi_t$) describing systems in non-equilibrium steady states (NESS).

**Key observables.** Entropy production rate ($\sigma$), probability current ($J$), local mean velocity ($v(x)$), connected correlation matrix $C(t)$, and the score function $s(x) = 
abla\ln ho(x)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Diffusion tensor ($D$), system dimensionality, and the degree of observation completeness (partial observation).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The dynamics are assumed to follow general overdamped diffusive processes, and the decomposition $\sigma = 4T + G$ is utilized.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the CYNAR pipeline, details the kinetic decomposition ($\sigma = 4T + G$), compares its performance against standard probability current estimation methods on various complex systems, and highlights the superior robustness and theoretical advantages of the CYNAR approach.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Inferring the entropy production rate $σ$ from recorded trajectories is a key challenge in stochastic thermodynamics. In experiments, the forces governing the dynamics are usually unknown and often only some of the system's degrees of freedom can be observed. Building on a recently introduced method [I. Di Terlizzi, Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 237101 (2025)], we develop and validate CYNAR (computation yields nonequilibrium analysis and reconstruction), a pipeline that estimates $σ$ from trajectories. It exploits a kinetic decomposition of $σ$ into a traffic term ${\cal T}$, inferred from the short-time curvature of correlation functions, and an inflow rate ${\cal G}$, computed from the steady-state score, i.e., the gradient of the log-density. We show that the same decomposition, evaluated on any subset of observed coordinates, always bounds $σ$ from below, for any diffusion tensor and without knowledge of the hidden degrees of freedom. We then compare CYNAR with a more standard approach that estimates $σ$ from steady-state probability currents, on four systems of increasing complexity. CYNAR proves to be more reliable, with no detectable bias close to equilibrium, weak dependence on spatial discretization, and marked robustness to measurement noise. It is also readily applicable to high-dimensional systems, where the traffic alone provides a lower bound close to $σ$, and remains informative under partial observation, including cases where the flux-based estimate vanishes identically. CYNAR is provided as an open-source Python package.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper quantifies how thermal fluctuations in a solid substrate enhance the friction experienced by ions in an electrolyte confined at the interface. By combining molecular dynamics with fluctuation-dissipation theory, the authors show that collective ionic modes dominate this friction, suggesting that understanding these many-body effects is key for applications like desalination and energy conversion.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides a detailed theoretical framework for calculating friction arising from collective many-body fluctuations, which is highly relevant to understanding energy dissipation in confined quantum systems or interfaces where many-body correlations are crucial.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how the internal thermal fluctuations of a solid substrate affect the friction experienced by ions moving through an electrolyte confined at the solid-electrolyte interface.

**Main result.** The ionic contribution to the interfacial friction is dominated by collective ionic modes, indicating that the friction arises from many-body interactions rather than simple individual drag forces.

**Method.** The authors combine theoretical modeling using the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem (FDT) with molecular dynamics simulations to calculate the fluctuation-induced friction coefficient.

**Model / system.** The system is a solid-electrolyte interface, modeled using a 2D nanochannel containing an electrolyte (e.g., NaCl). Solid excitations are incorporated via Drude oscillators, and the liquid response is derived from charge-density dynamical structure factors.

**Key observables.** Interfacial friction coefficient ($\lambda_{	ext{eff}}$), solid and liquid surface response functions ($	ext{Im}[g_{	ext{dr}}]$, $	ext{Im}[g_{\ell}]$), and the ionic contribution to friction ($\lambda_{	ext{FI}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Low-frequency regime, high-frequency molecular modes, and electrolyte concentration (e.g., 6.4 M NaCl).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The non-equilibrium MD approach is preferred over Green-Kubo methods due to rapid force auto-correlation decay, and the analysis relies on perturbation theory involving spectral overlaps.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the simulation setup, the comparison of $	ext{Im}[g_{	ext{dr}}]$ and $	ext{Im}[g_{\ell}]$ for pure water versus electrolyte, and plots showing the calculated effective friction coefficient enhancement.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by establishing the theoretical framework using FDT and perturbation theory, calculating the friction enhancement, and then comparing results from different theoretical models (like Debye-cloud and hydration modes) against non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this article, we explore how transport at a solid--electrolyte interface is affected by the internal fluctuations of the solid and quantify the role of solid excitations on ionic friction. Combining molecular dynamics simulations with theoretical modeling, we show that the presence of ions enhances the dynamical response of the electrolyte compared to pure water. This leads to an ionic contribution to the fluctuation-induced interfacial friction. We show that collective ionic modes dominate the dissipation, such that ionic friction arises from many-body effects rather than from individual drag forces. Furthermore, high-frequency molecular modes are found to be ion-specific, suggesting possible routes toward spectral separation of ions, with implications for desalination, filtration, and energy conversion.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents an all-optical, iterative scheme to deterministically generate large-amplitude squeezed cat states, which are vital resource states for fault-tolerant quantum computation using the GKP code. By employing quantum non-demolition interactions and photon-number measurements, the method achieves near-unity preparation probability and remains robust against photon loss. This paves a more realistic path toward implementing bosonic quantum error correction in photonic systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the hardware bottleneck for continuous-variable quantum computing by providing a high-fidelity, scalable method for generating necessary resource states (cat states) in photonics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is deterministically preparing large-amplitude squeezed cat states, which are crucial resource states for fault-tolerant quantum computation using the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code.

**Main result.** The authors propose an all-optical, iterative scheme that achieves the preparation of large-amplitude cat states with near-unity probability and demonstrates robustness against realistic photon loss.

**Method.** The scheme utilizes repeated quantum non-demolition (QND) interactions and photon-number measurements to amplify the initial cat state deterministically.

**Model / system.** The work is situated in photonic quantum computation, focusing on generating cat states via iterative amplification loops involving QND interactions and photon-number resolving (PNR) detectors.

**Key observables.** Fidelity ($F$) of the output state relative to the ideal cat state, success probability ($P_{	ext{success}}$) of reaching a photon number threshold ($n_t$), and effective squeezing metrics for GKP breeding.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of amplification rounds ($N$), the level of photon loss ($\ell$), and the required squeezing level ($r$) are key parameters analyzed.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the feasibility of high-efficiency QND interactions and PNR detection, and models the process by tracing over measured modes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the process flow, Wigner functions of the generated states, and comparative plots showing success probabilities and effective loss scaling for different amplification schemes.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theory by first proposing the iterative QND amplification scheme, then deriving the fidelity and success probabilities analytically, and finally applying these results to quantify the required squeezing for GKP state preparation.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill encoding has emerged as a leading candidate for fault-tolerant quantum computation with continuous variables. For photonic architectures, the major challenge is preparing high-quality resource states, which can be deterministically synthesised from many large-amplitude cat states. Thus far, only modest-sized optical cat states have been prepared experimentally, and the implemented methods are highly probabilistic. We propose an all-optical scheme utilising quantum non-demolition interactions and photon-number measurements to prepare large-amplitude cat states with near-unity probability. Importantly, no particular photon-number outcome is postselected: all outcomes contribute to the accumulated photon number, with the protocol repeated until a required threshold is reached. We demonstrate that the scheme is robust to realistic levels of photon-loss, the dominant source of error in optical systems. Our results highlight the power of active Gaussian operations for state preparation and pave the way for efficient quantum error correction using bosonic codes.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a method to reverse the stochastic diffusion process that describes open quantum system evolution. By deriving a backward stochastic differential equation on the manifold of pure states, the authors create a generative model for quantum states. This is significant because it allows for the controlled generation of quantum ensembles by reversing the effects of quantum dissipation.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous, geometrically motivated framework for simulating quantum processes in reverse, which is highly relevant for understanding quantum state preparation and noise characterization in open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper derives the time reversal of quantum state diffusion, which is governed by a Lindblad master equation, and utilizes this reversal for generating new quantum state ensembles.

**Main result.** A physical, nonlinear backward stochastic differential equation (SDE) is derived that unravels the inverse Lindbladian evolution, allowing for the generation of new quantum states from a prior distribution.

**Method.** The authors employ general machinery for stochastic differential equations on Riemannian manifolds, specifically working on the complex projective space of pure states, and comparing discrete-time approximations to the continuous backward SDE.

**Model / system.** The system is an open quantum system whose dynamics are described by a Lindblad master equation. The evolution of the pure state vector is modeled by Gisin's quantum state diffusion SDE.

**Key observables.** The probability density on the manifold of pure states, the relative entropy (KL divergence) between generated and original distributions, and the expectation value of an operator.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The Lindblad operators ($L_k$), the time step ($\delta$), and the structure of the noise fields.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation assumes the manifold of pure states is compact and smooth, and the backward SDE is only valid for the specific ensemble from which it was constructed.

**Figures summary.** The notes do not provide a summary of figures, but mention numerical tests for invariant ensembles using Jacobi polynomials.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the forward diffusion process via the Lindblad equation, to deriving the general formalism for time reversal on a Riemannian manifold, and finally applying this to derive error bounds and compare discrete vs. continuous time results.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum state diffusion unravels a Lindblad master equation into stochastic trajectories of pure states. The ensemble of trajectories is described by a probability density on the manifold of pure states, which contains much more information than the density matrix, its first moment. We derive the time reversal of this diffusion. Writing the reversal of a general diffusion on a manifold in Stratonovich form, and passing through the manifold of pure states, we obtain a backward stochastic differential equation for the state vector, valid for any Hilbert space dimension and any Lindbladian. The backward stochastic equation provides a physical, nonlinear unravelling of the inverse Lindbladian that holds only for the ensemble from which it was constructed. Following score-based generative models, we then use the backward equation to generate a new ensemble close to the original. For the depolarizing channel the unravelling is a Brownian motion on complex projective space, so the uniform distribution of pure states is its stationary law in any dimension. Starting the backward equation from that prior, we bound the error of the resulting distribution compared to the original one in different settings: exact and learned scores, continuous and discrete time.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops an efficient quantum information protocol to reconstruct a fermionic magic state $|\Psiangle$ that results from an unknown free-fermion evolution $\hat{U}$ acting on a structured input state $|\Psi_{	ext{in}}angle$. It achieves this by leveraging the spectral properties of particle reduced density matrices (RDMs) to decompose the state into its constituent blocks. The result demonstrates that the state can be learned with polynomial complexity, providing a powerful tool for characterizing complex quantum many-body states.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous theoretical framework for characterizing and simulating complex quantum states generated by free-fermion dynamics, which is highly relevant for understanding quantum simulation algorithms and resource estimation in quantum information.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper establishes efficient methods to learn a compact description of a fermionic magic state $|\Psiangle$ that results from applying an unknown free-fermion evolution ($\hat{U}$) to a structured input state $|\Psi_{	ext{in}}angle$.

**Main result.** The authors show that this learning can be achieved using single-copy measurements and polynomial complexity by exploiting the spectral structure of particle reduced density matrices (RDMs).

**Method.** The core method involves recursively analyzing and reconstructing the state by utilizing the $k$-RDM ($\Gamma^{(k)}$) to separate contributions from different input blocks, followed by classical post-processing like Gram-splitting.

**Model / system.** The system is a fermionic model described by creation and annihilation operators ($\hat{c}^\dagger, \hat{c}$) acting on $m$ modes. The state $|\Psiangle$ is generated by a passive Gaussian unitary $\hat{U}$ acting on a structured input state $|\Psi_{	ext{in}}angle$ composed of disjoint fermionic blocks.

**Key observables.** Particle reduced density matrices ($\Gamma^{(k)}_\Psi$), fidelity ($\epsilon_{	ext{fid}}$), and the reconstructed state $	ilde{\Psi}$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The required RDM order ($r$) is bounded by the maximum particle number per block; complexity depends polynomially on $m$ and $1/\epsilon_{	ext{fid}}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The input blocks have a definite, bounded particle number, and the analysis relies on the spectral properties of the RDMs to decompose the state structure.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the input state family ($\vert\Psi_{	ext{in}}angle$) and the target state ($\vert\Psiangle$), showing how local mode sets define blocks and how the target state is obtained via the unitary $\hat{U}$.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the problem (learning $\hat{U}|\Psi_{	ext{in}}angle$) to developing the mathematical tools (exploiting RDM spectral structure), proving the existence of efficient algorithms for both homogeneous and heterogeneous block structures, and finally bounding the preparation error and complexity.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We establish efficient learning for a family of fermionic magic states under unknown number-conserving free-fermion evolution. Each input block has a definite particle number and is a superposition of Fock states, with occupied mode sets disjoint both within and across blocks. The key idea is to exploit the spectral structure of particle reduced density matrices (RDMs) to separate contributions from individual blocks from those involving several blocks, allowing us to reconstruct the hidden block structure. For a fixed upper bound on the particle number per block, our algorithm uses single-copy measurements and polynomial sample and classical computational complexity to recover a compact description of the state with prescribed fidelity and high probability, without prior knowledge of the block decomposition or the evolution. RDMs up to this upper bound suffice for reconstruction. We further show that this RDM order is necessary in general: two orthogonal states in the family can have identical RDMs at every lower order. These results show that an extensive number of non-Gaussian blocks can be compatible with efficient state learning.

</details>

**Summary.** This work reports on magnetotransport measurements in graphene patterned with antidot lattices to study quantum geometric phases. The authors demonstrate that these engineered superlattices create moiré-like electronic structures in single-layer graphene. This establishes a clean, scalable platform for realizing and measuring fundamental quantum phenomena in 2D materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** The ability to engineer moiré physics in a single layer via lithography, rather than relying on complex stacking or twisting, provides a highly controllable platform for studying geometric phases relevant to topological physics and quantum transport.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the emergence and direct measurement of intrinsic quantum geometric phases in graphene by engineering periodic potentials.

**Main result.** The patterned antidot lattice successfully generates moiré-like electronic spectra in single-layer graphene without requiring twist or multilayer stacking, establishing a tunable platform for exploring moiré physics.

**Method.** Magnetotransport measurements ($R_{xx}$ vs. magnetic field) are performed on lithographically patterned graphene samples.

**Model / system.** The physical system is encapsulated monolayer graphene patterned with ultra-high-quality periodic antidot lattices. The analysis combines classical commensurability features (Weiss peaks) with quantum interference effects (Brown-Zak oscillations).

**Key observables.** Longitudinal magnetoresistance ($R_{xx}$), commensurability peaks ($H_k$), and Brown-Zak oscillations.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Antidot diameters ($\Theta$) ranging from 50 nm to 300 nm; carrier mobility ($\mu$) $\sim 10^5 	ext{ cm}^2/	ext{Vs}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The intrinsic geometric phase is directly measurable and the patterned lattice acts as a clean, tunable superlattice potential.

**Figures summary.** Figures show device schematics, optical micrographs of the antidot lattice, and magnetoresistance ($R_{xx}$) measurements resolving distinct commensurability peaks ($H_k$).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from demonstrating the physical platform (patterned graphene) to measuring classical commensurability features, and finally observing quantum interference effects like Brown-Zak oscillations, confirming the geometric phase measurement.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In graphene and other two-dimensional materials, periodic modulations of the electron density can significantly alter the energy spectrum and transport properties. Here, we report magnetotransport measurements in encapsulated monolayer graphene with ultra-high-quality patterned periodic antidot lattices that preserve the intrinsic electronic properties of the material. This lithographically defined platform enables controlled access to commensurability and superlattice phenomena at length scales otherwise difficult to achieve. By systematically tuning the lattice dimensions, we reveal a hierarchy of classical commensurability features arising from cyclotron orbits with comparable radii that follow multiple classical trajectories, resulting in broadened resistance peaks beyond the conventional single-orbit picture. Superimposed on these features, we observe pronounced Brown-Zak oscillations arising from the quantum commensurability between the magnetic flux quantum and the unit cell of the engineered Bravais lattices. We demonstrate that the intrinsic geometric phase of our system is directly measurable and show a precise matching of the magnetic field periodicity to the lithographic periodic patterning, where moiré-like electronic spectra can be geometrically generated in single-layer graphene without the need for twist, lattice mismatch, or multilayer stacking. Our results establish nanopatterned graphene as a clean, tunable, and scalable platform for realizing and exploring moiré physics through on-demand real-space design

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper uses AdS/CFT holography to calculate how energy is transmitted across interfaces separating different quantum field theories in dimensions higher than two. It derives a general formula for the transmission coefficient, establishing a new result for higher-dimensional systems and demonstrating surprising universality in the result.

**Why it may be interesting.** While highly technical, the concept of energy transport across boundaries is fundamental to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and open quantum systems, providing a holographic tool to calculate transport coefficients.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the universal behavior of energy transmission across holographic conformal interfaces in general spacetime dimensions ($d>2$). It seeks to extend known 2D results to higher dimensions where scattering is more complex.

**Main result.** The authors derive a closed-form expression for the energy transmission coefficient, showing it is independent of the incidence angle and the profile of the incident perturbation within the studied class of geometries.

**Method.** The calculation employs gravitational holography, perturbing the metric and matter fields around a domain-wall geometry dual to an Interacting Conformal Field Theory (ICFT). The transmission coefficient is derived by analyzing the energy flux observable.

**Model / system.** The model involves a codimension-one defect separating two CFTs, dual to an AdS$_d$-sliced domain-wall geometry. Specific examples include the thin-brane model and Janus geometries.

**Key observables.** Energy transmission coefficient ($T_{L,R}$), stress-tensor two-point function coefficients ($C_{T,L,R}$), and the energy flux observable $E$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimensionality $d$, the warp factor $a(y)$, and the tension parameters ($\Sigma$) characterizing the interface.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is restricted to a broad class of AdS$_d$-sliced domain-wall geometries, and the calculation relies on treating sources as small perturbations ($\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$).

**Figures summary.** The notes mention figures illustrating the thin-brane transmission coefficient versus tension, showing both symmetric and asymmetric cases.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the calculation by first establishing the general metric and stress tensor VEVs using Fefferman-Graham expansions, then applying matching and scattering conditions at the interface to derive the final ratio for the transmission coefficient.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Energy transport across conformal interfaces is universal in two spacetime dimensions, but its higher-dimensional counterpart has remained largely unexplored. In higher dimensions, scattering can depend on additional kinematic data, such as the angle of incidence, and conformal symmetry is far less restrictive. We use gravitational holography to study this problem. For a broad class of AdS$_d$-sliced domain-wall geometries, we derive a closed-form expression for the energy transmission coefficient in terms of the bulk warp factor. Our formula reproduces known two-dimensional holographic results and extends them to arbitrary dimension. Within this class, we establish different aspects of higher-dimensional universality. In particular, we show that the transmission is independent of the incidence angle and of the profile of the incident perturbation. We also derive bounds on transmission controlled by central-charge-like quantities characterizing the number of degrees of freedom of the theories on the two sides of the interface. This provides the first explicit result for reflection and transmission across conformal interfaces in higher dimensions, where no CFT-based results are currently available.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a novel methodology to calculate thermal properties of quantum field theories, such as those found in lattice gauge theories, using only real-time quantum simulation data. By employing exact integral transforms and optimizing the reconstruction kernel, the authors enable the extraction of finite-temperature, finite-$	heta$, and finite-$\mu$ physics from a single set of measurements. This significantly advances the feasibility of simulating complex thermal states on quantum hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** The technique provides a powerful, resource-efficient bridge between real-time quantum simulation (a major focus in quantum computing) and equilibrium statistical mechanics calculations, which is highly relevant for studying thermalization and phase transitions in quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is reconstructing imaginary-time evolution (needed for thermal factors and Euclidean correlators) from real-time quantum simulations, especially for finite temperature, topological angle, and chemical potential.

**Main result.** The authors developed a method that allows a single real-time dataset to reconstruct targeted thermal physics parameters ($eta, 	au, \mu$) through classical post-processing, circumventing the need for explicit thermal state preparation.

**Method.** The technique uses exact integral transforms to map real-time quantum measurements onto imaginary-time evolution operators, optimizing the reconstruction kernel for faster convergence.

**Model / system.** The method is benchmarked on lattice Schwinger models (one- and two-flavor) within the context of lattice field theory, allowing the study of thermal properties in gauge theories.

**Key observables.** Partition functions, thermal traces, Euclidean correlators, topological charge ($\langle Q angle$), and chiral condensate ($\langle ar{\psi}\psi angle$).

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Imaginary-time evolution can be reconstructed from real-time quantum simulations using exact integral transforms. We identify the construction of Guo, Shibu, Lin, and Zhao as a continuous linear combination of Hamiltonian simulations and show that its slow $1/t_{\rm cut}$ convergence arises from a redundant kernel component. We extend the construction from pure-state matrix elements to thermal traces and correlators. One real-time dataset then reconstructs targeted inverse temperatures, Euclidean separations, and chemical potentials through classical post-processing, bringing finite-$(T,θ,μ)$ physics within reach of real-time quantum simulation without thermal-state preparation. We benchmark the method on one- and two-flavor lattice Schwinger models, including circuit-level simulations with depolarizing noise.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a thermodynamic framework to quantify the energy costs associated with Continuous Quantum Error Correction (CQEC). By treating the process as an information engine, the authors show that achieving higher logical fidelity necessitates an ever-increasing expenditure of energy from the feedback mechanism. This establishes a fundamental energy-precision trade-off for quantum computation.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a rigorous thermodynamic cost accounting for quantum control, linking fundamental concepts like energy dissipation and information processing limits to practical quantum error correction schemes.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the thermodynamic resources (energy, work, entropy) required by Continuous Quantum Error Correction (CQEC) protocols.

**Main result.** It establishes a direct, quantifiable trade-off: improving logical fidelity requires a continuously increasing energetic investment from the feedback controller, even after fidelity saturates.

**Method.** The analysis formulates CQEC as a non-equilibrium information engine, applying the first law of thermodynamics to the system's evolution governed by a stochastic master equation.

**Model / system.** The study models CQEC using the one-qubit Ahn-Doherty-Landahl (ADL) protocol and extends it to the three-qubit repetition code. The dynamics are described by a stochastic master equation incorporating system Hamiltonian evolution, noise, and continuous feedback.

**Key observables.** Logical Fidelity ($F$), Internal Energy ($U$), System-side Power ($P_{sys}$), Feedback Power ($P_{fb}$), and Conditional-State Entropy ($S(ho_c)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Feedback strength ($\Omega$), Noise rate ($\gamma$), Monitoring strength ($\kappa$), and system Hamiltonian parameters ($\Delta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis distinguishes between system-side energy transfer and controller-side work, treating the process as a genuine non-equilibrium thermodynamic process.

**Figures summary.** Figures summarize the evolution of logical codespace fidelity, asymptotic average system and feedback power costs, and the relationship between power cost and logical fidelity.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the thermodynamic framework for CQEC, first on a minimal one-qubit system, deriving the first law decomposition. It then extends this analysis to the three-qubit repetition code, demonstrating the energetic cost scaling with increasing feedback strength.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Continuous quantum error correction (CQEC) replaces discrete syndrome measurements and recovery operations with continuous syndrome extraction and real-time Hamiltonian feedback. Here we investigate the thermodynamic resources required by this process by formulating measurement-based continuous quantum error correction as an information engine. We distinguish the system-side power associated with energy transfer between the feedback field and the protected system from the controller-side power associated with the feedback Hamiltonian. The framework is first developed for the one-qubit Ahn-Doherty-Landahl (ADL) protocol and subsequently extended to the three-qubit repetition code under continuous stabilizer monitoring. Numerical simulations show that increasing the feedback strength improves the steady-state fidelity and reduces the conditional-state entropy, while both energetic contributions continue to increase in magnitude after the fidelity begins to saturate. These results expose a direct tradeoff between logical stabilization and the energetic resources required for continuous feedback, closely related to previously established energy--precision tradeoffs in quantum measurement and quantum-Zeno stabilization.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a novel, structural diagnostic tool to detect coherent crosstalk in quantum processors by analyzing the residual Pauli Transfer Matrix (PTM). It proves that only genuine two-qubit interactions generate a unique, measurable signature in the PTM's cross-weight structure. This signature is then read out using a quantum-native Pauli-graph measurement, providing a robust method to distinguish hardware crosstalk from simple calibration drift.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous, structural diagnostic tool for quantum hardware characterization that moves beyond simple scalar fidelity metrics, which is crucial for scaling quantum computation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the critical challenge of distinguishing between malicious coherent crosstalk (nonlocal interactions) and benign calibration drift (local noise) in multi-tenant quantum processors, especially when both result in the same average gate infidelity.

**Main result.** A structural verification framework based on the residual Pauli Transfer Matrix (PTM) and Pauli-graph Quantum Hadamard Edge Detection (QHED) was developed, proving that only true two-qubit interactions generate a detectable, non-zero cross-weight signature.

**Method.** The authors use a structural diagnostic based on the signed antisymmetric coupling within the PTM, which is shown to be an isometry for two-qubit interactions. This signature is then read out quantum-natively using an FRQI encoding and Pauli-graph QHED.

**Model / system.** The work applies to multi-tenant quantum processors, modeled using Pauli operators and characterized by the Pauli Transfer Matrix (PTM). The analysis focuses on distinguishing local, unital noise channels from coherent, non-local two-qubit interaction channels.

**Key observables.** The primary observable is the signed cross-weight vector $\mathbf{x}$ derived from the residual PTM, and the secondary, quantum-native readout is the Pauli-graph Edge Score $	ext{edge}(S)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Detection threshold $\lambda_{\min} \approx 0.13$ (for 16,384 settings), scaling $\propto M^{-1/2}$, and the first-order dependence on interaction strength $\lambda$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method assumes the ability to perform randomized-Pauli measurements and relies on the structural property that local errors yield zero cross-weight mass, while two-qubit interactions do not.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the detection pipeline from shared datasets to the residual PTM, the use of the cross-weight signature, and the final quantum-native readout via Pauli-graph QHED, confirming the detection limit scaling.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the ambiguity between crosstalk and drift using average fidelity, introduces the PTM framework to define a structural signature ($\mathbf{x}$), proves mathematically that this signature separates local from nonlocal errors, and finally implements a quantum-native readout using FRQI and QHED.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Multi-tenant quantum processors expose a pulse-level attack surface in which coherent crosstalk can mimic benign calibration drift at matched average gate infidelity. We present a structural verification and detection framework based on the residual Pauli transfer matrix (PTM). We prove that products of local unital, trace-preserving channels cannot mix weight-1 and weight-2 Pauli operators, even under coherent drift of arbitrary strength or axis. Building on established PTM-to-Hamiltonian relations, we prove that, for any specified qubit pair in an arbitrarily large system, the first-order map from its nine interaction coefficients to the antisymmetric cross-weight feature is an isometry up to scale. Thus, every interaction direction is locally observable near the identity. We also exhibit cancellation of this feature under large local rotations and prove that the full cross-weight norm is invariant under local unitary composition, providing a structural countermeasure. For calibrated small local rotations, shared randomized-Pauli measurements support periodic verification using the evaluated antisymmetric detector. In simulation, $16{,}384$ randomized settings yield a detection threshold of $λ_{\min}\approx0.13$ at a $5\%$ calibrated false-positive target, with approximately $M^{-1/2}$ scaling in the number of settings $M$. Further experiments characterize detection under relaxation, depolarization, native ZZ fluctuations, and time-dependent pulse dynamics. Finally, an FRQI encoding with Pauli-graph quantum Hadamard edge detection reproduces the classical structural edge score to numerical precision.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces 'Double Localization,' a novel mathematical framework to prove spectral gaps in quantum many-body systems. By combining global control over a defined 'interface' subspace with local gap estimates, the authors establish rigorous, size-independent lower bounds on the thermalization rate for specific Hamiltonians on structured graphs. This provides a significant theoretical advance for analyzing quantum thermalization dynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, generalizable mathematical tool (Double Localization) to prove spectral gaps in complex quantum systems, which is crucial for understanding thermalization rates in quantum simulation and quantum information processing.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is quantifying the rate at which a quantum many-body system approaches thermal equilibrium, which is diagnosed by proving a positive spectral gap for the quantum dynamics.

**Main result.** The authors prove an unconditional spectral-gap lower bound for the full dynamics, independent of graph size, for specific Hamiltonians derived from Kitaev's construction on finite graphs.

**Method.** They introduce and utilize a novel 'Double Localization' framework that combines a global bound on a defined 'interface' subspace with local quantum gap estimates under specific coupling and assembly conditions.

**Model / system.** The study applies to quantum many-body systems defined on finite, simple, three-regular graphs. The Hamiltonian is built from vertex terms of Kitaev’s finite-group quantum double construction, and the dynamics are governed by a local Davies process.

**Key observables.** Spectral Gap, Interface Subspace ($M$), Local Quantum Gap Estimates ($K_p$), and the Generator of the evolution.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Coupling Strength ($J$), Inverse Temperature ($eta$), and the structure of the finite group ($\Gamma$, e.g., $S_3$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The abstract theorem requires quantitative coupling and geometric assembly conditions, and the final results rely on specific bounds derived for the interface and local updates.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the conceptual framework: Figure 1 shows two perspectives (clustering/reduction), Figure 2 schematically details Double Localization (geometric vs. interface), and Figure 3 shows the assembly process combining global and local estimates to yield the full gap.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the abstract Double Localization gap theorem, applies it to the specific Hamiltonian model on finite graphs, and then provides detailed, rigorous calculations (including combinatorial counting and polynomial analysis) to establish the required positive bounds for the interface and local components.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We introduce double localization, a framework for proving spectral gaps of quantum Gibbs samplers through two complementary operations: geometric localization, which selects updates supported in small spatial regions, and interface localization, which focuses on a model-defined subspace of observables while remaining geometrically global. Our abstract gap theorem combines a global bound on this subspace, called the interface, with local quantum gap estimates under quantitative coupling and geometric assembly conditions. The resulting explicit lower bound controls the gap of the full dynamics without requiring the interface to be invariant under the generator. This separation allows global estimates, including classical comparison, to be combined with local control of the remaining quantum directions.   We apply the framework to Hamiltonians built from the vertex terms of Kitaev's finite-group quantum double construction, without plaquette terms, on finite simple three-regular graphs of girth at least six. For the specified local Davies dynamics, we prove an unconditional spectral-gap lower bound by a positive constant independent of graph size for every fixed nontrivial finite group and each fixed inverse temperature $β$ with $0\leβJ<\log(5/3)$, where $J>0$ is the coupling strength. For the smallest non-Abelian group $S_3$, double localization yields a positive lower bound uniform in both graph size and the entire interval $0\leβJ\le\log 3$, providing a guarantee that does not follow directly from existing results. This demonstrates how model-specific finite calculations can extend spectral-gap guarantees for the full quantum dynamics.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents advanced classical algorithms to simulate free-fermion dynamics, particularly when the initial state is non-Gaussian. It achieves efficient computation for sampling the output state and estimating various expectation values by exploiting the block-product structure of the input. These results offer significant classical benchmarks for simulating fermionic quantum circuits relevant to trapped-ion quantum computing.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides concrete, efficient classical benchmarks for simulating complex fermionic quantum processes, directly impacting the feasibility assessment of quantum hardware simulations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing fast classical simulation algorithms for free-fermion dynamics, especially when the input state is non-Gaussian.

**Main result.** The authors provide exact sampling algorithms for free-fermion dynamics with input states composed of magic states, achieving polynomial time for certain expectation values and improving upon prior quasi-polynomial runtimes.

**Method.** The work develops specialized classical algorithms leveraging Gaussian state decompositions, dynamic programming, and recursive sampling theorems tailored for block-product input states.

**Model / system.** The focus is on free-fermion circuits governed by quadratic Hamiltonians, simulating dynamics applied to input states formed by products of four-mode magic states, relevant to trapped-ion experiments.

**Key observables.** Full output distribution (Fock basis samples), number correlators, and expectation values of Majorana monomials.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The input state structure (products of even-parity blocks), the desired accuracy ($\epsilon$), and the failure probability ($\delta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The algorithms assume the input blocks are pure and possess even parity; the additive-error runtimes exclude a one-time polynomial-time preprocessing step.

**Figures summary.** Not specified, but the notes reference a TABLE I summarizing various algorithm runtimes for different tasks (Sampling, Expectation value, Overlap).

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically develops algorithms for three tasks: exact sampling, expectation value computation, and additive-error estimation, building upon the block-product structure of the input state and utilizing advanced techniques like Gaussian decomposition and dynamic programming.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The classical cost of simulating free-fermion (matchgate) circuits depends on both the input state and the computational task. We develop classical algorithms for circuits with non-Gaussian inputs, addressing exact sampling and both additive-error and exact estimation of expectation values. For inputs consisting of $n$ copies of the four-mode magic state, we give exact sampling algorithms, generalizing the Clifford and Clifford algorithm for Boson sampling, for passive and active free-fermion dynamics with worst-case arithmetic cost $O(2^n)$ per sample, without any multiplicative polynomial prefactor. The passive algorithm enables an exact simulation of the non-interacting regime of a recent trapped-ion experiment. We also extend recently developed additive-error estimation of number correlators and related observables from passive to active dynamics with runtime polynomial in $n$ and the inverse additive-error, for input states formed by products of $n$ four-mode even parity states. Our estimator uses a Gaussian-state decomposition adapted to each sampled state to control its second moment. This includes estimation of individual output probabilities. Finally, we show that for even-parity product inputs composed of constant-size blocks, expectation values of Majorana monomials of logarithmic weight can be computed exactly in polynomial time, improving on prior Majorana propagation-style algorithms with quasi-polynomial runtime. The exact algorithm processes the input blocks by dynamic programming, sharing calculations across subsets of Majorana factors. Our suite of algorithms provide classical benchmarks for fermionic quantum simulations across a broad spectrum of computational tasks.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper provides a deep mathematical introduction to Many-Body Localization (MBL), a phenomenon where quantum systems fail to thermalize due to disorder. It details the theoretical framework, contrasting MBL's memory retention against thermal expectations using diagnostics like entanglement entropy and level statistics. The core mathematical effort involves developing rigorous renormalization and probabilistic techniques to prove the stability of MBL against perturbations.

**Why it may be interesting.** MBL is a major topic in non-equilibrium quantum dynamics, directly impacting how we model thermalization and memory retention in complex quantum materials, which is highly relevant to AMO physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses Many-Body Localization (MBL), which describes how isolated quantum systems can fail to reach thermal equilibrium, violating the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH). It seeks to provide a rigorous mathematical understanding of this phenomenon.

**Main result.** The notes outline advanced mathematical techniques, including renormalization group flow and probabilistic estimates, required to prove MBL persists over a range of weak, generic local perturbations.

**Method.** The analysis employs sophisticated mathematical tools like the Schrieffer–Wolff transformation, renormalization schemes, and probabilistic bounding techniques (e.g., fractional moments) to control the growth of perturbative terms.

**Model / system.** The focus is on quantum spin-1/2 chains with random disorder, described by Hamiltonians $H = \sum h_i Z_i + 	ext{interactions}$. The system is studied in the context of its deviation from thermalizing behavior.

**Key observables.** Local observables, entanglement entropy (area vs. volume law), level statistics (Poisson vs. GOE), and the existence of quasi-local conserved quantities (LIOMs).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The disorder strength ($h_i$), the coupling constant ($\gamma$), and the system size ($L$). The analysis is sensitive to the ratio of coupling to energy gaps.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the assumption of a quasi-local unitary transformation $U$ and aims to prove results holding with high probability, often assuming non-resonance conditions.

**Paper structure.** The structure progresses from introducing the physical conflict (MBL vs. ETH) to developing mathematical diagnostics (level statistics, entanglement entropy), and finally detailing the advanced mathematical machinery (Schrieffer-Wolff, renormalization, probabilistic bounds) needed for a rigorous proof of stability.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

These notes are based on a mini-course delivered at the Les Houches Summer School, Quantum Theory on All Scales, in August 2026. They introduce many-body localization to mathematicians, emphasizing the physical mechanisms that support or destabilize it. The mathematical discussion deals with how perturbative rotations, renormalization, and probabilistic estimates are used in a rigorous approach to many-body localization.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a breakthrough protocol for quantum double lock-in detection, enabling the simultaneous measurement of a signal's amplitude, frequency, and phase using only one quantum interferometer. By employing sequential orthogonal pulses and utilizing entangled GHZ states, the technique achieves Heisenberg-limited precision, significantly surpassing classical and standard quantum limits.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum optics as it proposes a resource-efficient, high-precision measurement technique for oscillating signals using collective spin systems (like trapped ions or atoms).

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of achieving high-precision quantum double lock-in detection—which requires measuring signal amplitude, frequency, and initial phase—using minimal experimental resources.

**Main result.** A novel protocol using a single quantum interferometry, specifically with Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states, allows measurement precisions to approach the Heisenberg limit ($\propto 1/N$).

**Method.** The method involves a three-stage quantum sensing protocol: initialization, interrogation via sequential orthogonal periodic multipulse sequences (PDD and CP), and final readout.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled using an ensemble of N two-state bosonic particles, described by collective spin operators ($\hat{J}_x, \hat{J}_y, \hat{J}_z$) and governed by a Hamiltonian incorporating the oscillating signal and reference pulses.

**Key observables.** The half-population difference $\langle J_z angle_f$ is the primary observable, analyzed via Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) or Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) to locate the lock-in point.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The measurement precision scales with $N$ (particle number), aiming for the Heisenberg Limit ($1/N$) over the Standard Quantum Limit ($1/\sqrt{N}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The protocol assumes the ability to execute ideal $\pi$-pulses and analyzes robustness against systematic detuning and rotation angle errors.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the three stages of the detection scheme. Figure 2 shows FFT/IPR spectra confirming lock-in detection. Figure 3 compares measurement precision scaling ($\Delta A, \Delta\omega, \Deltaeta$) vs. $N$ for both individual and GHZ states. Figure 5 shows scaling under detection noise.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the problem and the single-interferometry protocol. It details the mathematical framework using sequential pulses, analyzes the measurement observables (SCS vs. GHZ states), demonstrates the scaling improvement to the Heisenberg limit, and finally proves the scheme's robustness against common experimental noise sources.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

High-precision measurement of oscillating signal is a ubiquitous issue in fundamental science and a critical task in practical technologies. In quantum metrology, quantum lock-in detection provide an efficient method for measuring such signal. In general, when the initial phase of the oscillating signal is unknown,quantum double lock-in detection can effectively extract complete information about the signal's amplitude, frequency, and initial phase. Conventional quantum double lock-in detection requires two individual quantum interferometry, each of which must undergo state preparation and readout. However, the time for state preparation and readout need not be negligible in practical experiments. In particular, the time for state preparation is longer than the time for sensing. To save experimental resources, it is challenging to achieve quantum double lock-in detection just via a single quantum interferometry while still extracting complete information about the signal's amplitude, frequency, and initial phase. Here, we present a general protocol for achieving a quantum double lock-in detection just via a single quantum interferometry under a sequential orthogonal periodic multipulse sequences. In particular, if the input state is a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state and two interaction-based operations are applied during interferometry, the measurement precisions for frequency, amplitude, and initial phase can both approach the Heisenberg limit. Our study paves a new way for measuring oscillating signals with a single quantum interferometry, and provides a feasible method for achieving Heisenberg-limited detection of alternating signals.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces time-integrated leakage as a necessary metric for evaluating superconducting-qubit reset protocols, arguing that final residual population alone is insufficient. By simulating a complex multi-mode system, the authors demonstrate that transient leakage can reveal performance limitations missed by endpoint measurements. This is vital knowledge for designing robust quantum error correction cycles.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a rigorous, quantitative framework for analyzing open quantum system dynamics in superconducting circuits, moving beyond simple steady-state measurements to characterize the entire reset trajectory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the limitation of using only the final residual population to characterize superconducting-qubit reset performance, proposing time-integrated leakage as a superior metric.

**Main result.** Time-integrated leakage ($L_f$) is a crucial diagnostic tool, as it can reveal performance bottlenecks missed by endpoint measurements, especially when comparing different reset protocols.

**Method.** The authors use numerical simulations solving the master equation for a multi-mode superconducting qubit system under flux control and dissipation.

**Model / system.** The system is a superconducting transmon qubit coupled to a multi-mode auxiliary chain and a lossy resonator, modeled using a Lindblad master equation approach.

**Key observables.** Time-integrated leakage ($L_f$), final residual populations ($P_f(t_f)$), and sustained threshold times ($t_s(\epsilon)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Thermal occupation ($ar{n}$), frequency disorder ($\Delta$), and the coupling strength of the auxiliary chain.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The dissipative model is effective and not fully device-calibrated; the comparison to literature rate models is explicitly noted as a kinetic reference only.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the qubit architecture, and subsequent figures show trends of residual leakage and population versus disorder strength or thermal occupation.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem by comparing metrics, details the multi-mode dissipative model, presents ablation studies comparing different circuit components, and concludes by advocating for the use of time-integrated leakage in error correction contexts.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Reset performance in superconducting qubits is often summarized by the population that remains at the end of the pulse. This is an important number, but it does not describe what happens during the reset itself. A protocol may reach a small final residual while keeping the qubit in a leakage state for a comparatively long part of the trajectory. In this work, we therefore use time-integrated leakage, together with the usual endpoint population, to study a multi-mode dissipative reset model under flux-frequency control. We examine finite thermal occupation, parameter sweeps, frequency disorder, an auxiliary-chain ablation, and a literature-based rate benchmark. At the representative ablation point, adding the auxiliary chain reduces Lf from 8.56 to 0.78 ns and shifts the sustained Pf less-than- 10-2 crossing from 39.5 to 9.8 ns. Interestingly, the configuration without the chain still reaches the smaller long-time residual. The two metrics can therefore favor different reset configurations. For the same 300 ns analysis window, an effective rate model built from the f-ket and e-ket decay rates reported by Zhou et al. gives Lf is 108.0 ns, while the complete simulated configuration gives 0.783 ns. We use this only as a kinetic reference and not as a reproduction of the experiment. In the wider set of simulations, thermal occupation is the main source of degradation, while the frequency disorder considered here has a much weaker effect. The results suggest that time-integrated leakage is a useful quantity to report alongside endpoint residuals, especially when reset is part of repeated quantum-error-correction cycles.

</details>
