**Summary.** This work analyzes the sample complexity in Quantum PAC learning, determining the necessary amount of quantum data required to learn a function from an unknown distribution. The authors prove that restricting access to only the forward state-preparation unitary (and not its inverse) does not yield an asymptotic advantage over classical or copy-based quantum learning in the worst case. This establishes the essential role of inverse access in achieving known quantum improvements.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides rigorous theoretical limits on the power of quantum access protocols, specifically quantifying the necessity of inverse access for achieving known quantum advantages in machine learning settings.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates whether quantum computation can reduce the sample complexity required to learn a prediction rule compared to classical learning.

**Main result.** In the worst-case setting, forward-only access to a state-preparation unitary cannot provide an asymptotic query-complexity advantage over learning from classical data or quantum data copies.

**Method.** The authors establish lower bounds using a reduction that approximates the Haar-averaged output of any $q$-query forward-only algorithm using $q$ copies of the prepared state.

**Model / system.** The study uses the Quantum PAC learning framework, where unknown probability distributions are encoded in quantum states. The learning task is analyzed under different access models: quantum data copies, or forward-only access to a state-preparation unitary $U$.

**Key observables.** Query complexity ($q$), sample complexity, and the resulting lower bounds for realizable and agnostic learning.

**Important parameters / regimes.** VC dimension ($d$), accuracy parameter ($\epsilon$), and failure probability ($\delta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis takes the worst case over compatible state-preparation unitaries and their finite ambient dimensions.

**Figures summary.** A table summarizes PAC learning complexity across different access models, highlighting the derived lower bounds for forward-only access.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by establishing the necessary theoretical tools, including a reduction theorem that connects forward-query lower bounds to copy-based lower bounds, culminating in the derivation of the final complexity bounds.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Whether quantum computation can reduce the amount of data sampled from an unknown probability distribution required to learn a prediction rule is a fundamental question in quantum machine learning. Quantum PAC learning studies this question using quantum data as a quantum state whose squared amplitudes encode the unknown distribution from which classical learning data are sampled. With only copies of such quantum data, the optimal worst-case sample complexity asymptotically matches that of classical PAC learning. In contrast, access to both a state-preparation unitary for this state and its inverse can improve the query-complexity dependence on the accuracy parameter in realizable learning. However, it has remained unclear whether forward-only access allows such an improvement.   In this work, taking the worst case over compatible state-preparation unitaries and their finite ambient dimensions, we show that the optimal forward-only query complexities of realizable and agnostic learning are, respectively, $Θ((d+\log(1/δ))/\varepsilon)$ and $Θ((d+\log(1/δ))/\varepsilon^2)$, where $d$ is the VC dimension of the concept class, $\varepsilon$ the accuracy parameter, and $δ$ the failure probability. These bounds match the optimal sample complexities with classical data or quantum data copies. To prove them, we establish a reduction using $q$ copies of the prepared state to approximate the Haar-averaged output of any $q$-query forward-only algorithm.   These results show that forward-only access cannot provide an asymptotic query-complexity advantage over learning from classical data or quantum data copies in this worst-case setting, and establish the essential role of inverse access in the known realizable-setting improvement. Our reduction also provides a new framework for analyzing limitations of forward state-preparation access via state-copy lower bounds.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proves that any arbitrary unitary transformation on $n$ qubits can be implemented by a quantum circuit of constant depth, up to an approximation error $\epsilon$. This is achieved by leveraging deep connections between quantum computation, coding theory, and complexity theory. The result suggests that quantum time evolution can be highly parallelized, a significant theoretical advance for quantum circuit design.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a powerful theoretical result showing that the time complexity (depth) of universal quantum computation can be drastically reduced to constant depth, provided sufficient ancillary resources (space) are available.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Determining the minimum circuit depth required to implement an arbitrary n-qubit unitary operation.

**Main result.** All n-qubit unitaries can be approximated to any desired precision $\epsilon$ by a quantum circuit of constant depth, provided the use of exponential-sized quantum fan-out gates is allowed.

**Method.** The proof connects unitary synthesis to locally-decodable codes and private information retrieval, utilizing a three-query quantum algorithm structure derived from continuous-variable quantum computation.

**Model / system.** The analysis focuses on the abstract implementation of unitary matrices $U \in U(N)$ acting on $N$ qubits, initially modeled using continuous states of a quantum harmonic oscillator.

**Key observables.** Operator norm error $\epsilon$, circuit depth (aiming for constant depth), and circuit width (scaling polynomially with $N$ and logarithmically with $1/\epsilon$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Number of qubits $N$, approximation error $\epsilon$, and the required number of ancilla qubits ($2^{O(n)}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The final constant-depth result requires the allowance of quantum fan-out gates, and the initial construction relies on continuous-variable quantum computation which is then discretized.

**Figures summary.** Not specified, but the notes describe algorithmic steps involving encoding isometries, diagonal phase queries, and the Quantum Fourier Transform.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from the general problem of unitary synthesis to specific algorithmic components (encoding, phase query, QFT) and culminates in showing that these components can be combined into a constant-depth circuit.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

It is well-known that every $n$-qubit unitary can be implemented by a $2^{O(n)}$-depth quantum circuit using single- and two-qubit gates. It has been open whether exponential depth is \emph{necessary} for general unitaries, even when allowing for unlimited number of ancilla qubits. We show, perhaps surprisingly, that all unitaries can be approximated to operator norm $ε$ by a circuit of one- and two-qubit gates of depth $\poly(n,\log 1/ε)$ with $2^{O(n)}$ ancilla qubits. In other words, every $n$-qubit unitary can be parallelized to polynomial depth. Moreover, if we allow unbounded fan-out gates, these circuits can be reduced further to \emph{constant} depth. Our construction takes advantage of a novel relationship connecting the unitary synthesis problem of Aaronson and Kuperberg to locally-decodable codes and private information retrieval from complexity theory and cryptography.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes the convergence rates of quantum optimization algorithms for finding Nash equilibria in zero-sum games. It proves that the average-iterate convergence rate is fundamentally limited by $\Omega(1/\epsilon)$. Furthermore, it establishes specific polynomial decay rates for the last iterate using explicit quantum game constructions, distinguishing between average and last-iterate performance.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides rigorous lower bounds on the convergence speed for quantum game theory algorithms, which is crucial for understanding the fundamental limits of quantum optimization protocols.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the convergence rates for finding approximate Nash equilibria in quantum zero-sum games using optimistic matrix mirror-prox methods.

**Main result.** It establishes lower bounds showing that the average-iterate convergence for the uniform average output is $\Omega(1/\epsilon)$, and demonstrates polynomial convergence rates ($\Theta(1/t)$ or $\Theta(1/t^2)$) for the last iterate using specific fixed games.

**Method.** The analysis employs theoretical tools comparing average-iterate guarantees against last-iterate convergence rates for algorithms like OGDA and OMMWU, using explicit constructions on one-qubit games.

**Model / system.** The model is quantum zero-sum games, where players act on density matrices (states) defined on a spectraplex, explicitly constructed using one qubit per player.

**Key observables.** $\epsilon$-Nash equilibrium approximation, average-iterate guarantee, last-iterate Frobenius distance, duality gap, and quantum relative entropy.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Accuracy parameter $\epsilon$, number of iterations $t$, and step size $\eta$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis distinguishes between the rate achieved by the uniform average versus the rate achieved by the last iterate, and the lower bounds are based on games where equilibria have singular strategies.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the decay of the duality gap and distance to equilibrium for OGDA and OMMWU on specific fixed games, comparing different initializations.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the average-iterate lower bound, then analyzing the last-iterate convergence for OGDA and OMMWU on fixed games, contrasting the decay rates for different error measures.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Optimistic matrix mirror-prox (OMMP) computes $ε$-approximate Nash equilibria in quantum zero-sum games with an $O(1/\varepsilon)$ average-iterate guarantee [arXiv:2311.10859]. We investigate whether this dependence on accuracy is tight and whether geometric last-iterate convergence can be guaranteed. We study these questions through explicit games with one qubit per player. First, we prove an $Ω(1/\varepsilon)$ lower bound for the uniform-average output that includes the maximally mixed initial state, independently of the regularizer and step size. Second, we construct a fixed game on which optimistic gradient descent-ascent (OGDA), initialized at the maximally mixed state, has last-iterate Frobenius distance to equilibrium $Θ(1/t)$ and duality gap $Θ(1/t^3)$ for every sufficiently small fixed step size. A separate fixed game exhibits arbitrarily long delays in reducing the initial error by a constant factor across a family of initial states. Finally, we give a fixed game with a unique, strictly complementary equilibrium on which optimistic matrix multiplicative weights updates (OMMWU) converge only polynomially from the maximally mixed state for every fixed positive step size. The last-iterate Frobenius distance and quantum relative entropy from the equilibrium to the iterates decay as $Θ(1/t)$, while the duality gap decays as $Θ(1/t^2)$.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops algorithms to simulate quantum error correction codes under coherent noise, specifically ZZ crosstalk on surface codes. While crosstalk alone is efficiently simulable, the combination of crosstalk and single-qubit noise proves to be computationally hard, suggesting a fundamental barrier to classical simulation unless major complexity assumptions fail.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work directly tackles the resource estimation and simulation limits for quantum error correction codes, which is central to understanding the feasibility of fault-tolerant quantum computation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the computational difficulty of classically simulating the syndrome distribution of surface codes when subjected to coherent nearest-neighbor ZZ crosstalk, especially when combined with single-qubit rotations.

**Main result.** An efficient polynomial-time algorithm exists for simulating crosstalk alone, but the combination of single-qubit rotations and crosstalk leads to a syndrome distribution that is computationally hard to sample from unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses.

**Method.** The authors use algorithmic techniques to sample the syndrome distribution $p(s)$ and analyze the resulting logical state $|\psi_sangle$ after syndrome-dependent Pauli correction.

**Model / system.** The system is a surface code, specifically on a rotated lattice, encoding one logical qubit into $d^2$ physical qubits. The noise model includes coherent nearest-neighbor ZZ crosstalk and single-qubit Z-rotations.

**Key observables.** Syndrome distribution $p(s)$, the resulting logical state $|\psi_sangle$, and the logical channel's diamond-norm distance from the identity.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The crosstalk angle $	heta_e$ and the single-qubit rotation angle $\phi$. Threshold extrapolations are provided for the critical angle $	heta_c/\pi$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The hardness result for combined noise assumes a multiplicative approximation guarantee. The analysis of crosstalk alone relies on the syndrome distribution factorizing into two independent standard codes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the surface code structure on rotated lattices, detailing physical qubits and stabilizer faces. Other figures show the construction of complex quantum circuits (king-lattice IQP circuits) used to embed computations.

**Paper structure.** The paper first presents an efficient algorithm for crosstalk alone, showing factorization. It then analyzes the combined noise, leading to a complexity-theoretic obstruction result. A separate, related section details the construction of complex quantum circuits to establish complexity class containments.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We give a polynomial-time classical algorithm which samples from the syndrome distribution of a surface code state corrupted by coherent nearest-neighbor $ZZ$ crosstalk. Our algorithm complements the known efficient simulation algorithms for coherent single-qubit errors in the surface code. When both single-qubit coherent noise and coherent crosstalk are present, we find a complexity-theoretic obstruction to efficient simulation: unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses, there is no efficient classical algorithm for sampling from the syndrome distribution, even up to a constant multiplicative error. This is obtained by connecting the syndrome distribution under coherent noise to the output distribution of certain IQP circuits associated with a non-planar graph.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously determines the complete set of product states that minimize the expectation value of a specific three-qubit entanglement witness. By using advanced algebraic methods like Gröbner basis computation, the authors prove that the witness is optimal because the minimizing states span the entire Hilbert space. This provides a precise, mathematically proven entanglement detection threshold for mixed states.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous mathematical characterization of entanglement witnesses using advanced algebraic geometry techniques provides a powerful theoretical tool for quantifying quantum correlations beyond simple separability criteria.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to determine the complete set of product states that minimize the expectation value of the canonical three-qubit Shifts witness, thereby proving the witness's optimality for detecting entanglement.

**Main result.** The complete equality set consists of exactly eight product rays, which span the entire three-qubit Hilbert space, confirming the witness's optimality. This establishes a precise entanglement detection threshold for white-noise mixtures.

**Method.** The analysis combines complex phase analysis, the classification of stationary points derived from setting the partial derivatives of the expectation value function to zero, and the use of Gröbner basis computation from commutative algebra.

**Model / system.** The system is a three-qubit quantum state space, analyzed using a witness operator ($W$) derived from the Shifts Unextendible Product Basis (UPB) projector. The goal is to characterize the boundary of the separable set.

**Key observables.** The minimum product-state expectation value $\lambda_{	ext{Shifts}} = 1 - 3\sqrt{6}/8$, and the white-noise detection threshold $p_W = 2 - 3\sqrt{6}/4$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of qubits (three), the specific structure of the Shifts UPB, and the mixing parameter $p$ for the white-noise family.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The proof relies on the assumption that any complex product state attaining equality must correspond to one of the analyzed real stationary points, and that the algebraic methods used (Gröbner basis) are complete.

**Figures summary.** Not specified in the notes, but the analysis involves classifying 28 finite real stationary points and analyzing projective boundaries.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the Shifts UPB and the witness (Section II), derives the symmetric equality rays (Section III), and finally establishes the complete classification of all minimizing rays using Gröbner basis elimination and boundary analysis (Section IV).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

For the three-qubit Shifts unextendible product basis (UPB), the minimum product-state expectation value $λ_{\mathrm{Shifts}}=1-3\sqrt6/8$ of the UPB projector is known, and four attaining product states were exhibited previously. We determine the complete equality set over all complex product states and prove that it consists of exactly eight product rays: two rays invariant under cyclic permutation of the three qubits and two cyclic orbits of size three. The proof combines exact phase analysis, a Gröbner-basis classification of all 28 finite real stationary points, and a complete treatment of the projective boundaries. Crucially, the eight contact rays span the full three-qubit Hilbert space, whereas the four previously known rays do not. The complete equality classification therefore establishes that the associated projector witness satisfies the spanning criterion and is optimal in the sense that no nonzero positive semidefinite operator can be subtracted while preserving block positivity. As a corollary, for the white-noise family $ρ(p)=(1-p)ρ_{\mathrm{Shifts}}+p\mathbb I/8$, where $ρ_{\mathrm{Shifts}}$ is the complementary-projector Shifts state, the same witness detects entanglement for $p<2-3\sqrt6/4\approx16.29\%$.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper demonstrates that in the presence of noise, standard quantum complexity diagnostics (like magic or scrambling) fail to reliably track the limits of efficient classical simulation. The separation is attributed to the fact that these diagnostics probe higher-order statistical moments than the moments relevant to the best classical simulation algorithms. This suggests that measuring such diagnostics on a noisy device is insufficient evidence for true quantum computational advantage.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly challenges the assumption that quantum complexity measures are universally reliable indicators of computational hardness, providing crucial theoretical nuance for assessing quantum advantage claims in realistic, noisy settings.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates whether standard quantum dynamical diagnostics (like magic or scrambling) reliably predict the limits of efficient classical simulation when quantum circuits are subjected to noise.

**Main result.** The diagnostics and classical simulability do not reliably track each other in noisy mixed-state circuits, as they probe different statistical moments that decay at different rates under noise.

**Method.** The authors compare the behavior of structural diagnostics (e.g., fourth-order moments) against the computational cost derived from best-known classical simulation algorithms (which often depend on second-order moments).

**Model / system.** The study analyzes noisy random quantum circuits, specifically two families: noisy Clifford+$T$ circuits and noisy matchgate circuits, subjected to local depolarizing noise.

**Key observables.** Magic, operator scrambling (OTOCs), anticoncentration, and fermionic non-Gaussianity are used as diagnostics, alongside the computational cost derived from classical simulation algorithms.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Noise strength, circuit depth, and system size ($N$) are key parameters used to map out the separation regimes.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The initial connection between diagnostics and simulability was established for noiseless circuits, and the analysis highlights that diagnostics measured on a noisy device do not constitute evidence for classical hardness by themselves.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 summarizes the central result, showing that the boundary where the resource diagnostic becomes trivial does not coincide with the boundary separating regions of efficient classical simulation for both circuit families.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theoretical framework by analyzing the statistical moments probed by various diagnostics and comparing these to the decay rates governing the efficiency of known classical simulation techniques for the specified noisy circuit models.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Claims of quantum advantage rest on the classical hardness of simulating quantum circuits. Magic, operator scrambling, anticoncentration, and non-Gaussianity for fermionic circuits are standard diagnostics of complex quantum dynamics. For pure states, some of these have been rigorously connected to classical simulability. Whether these diagnostics reliably track the limits of efficient classical simulation under noise remains unclear. Here, we show that in noisy Clifford+$T$ and nearest-neighbour matchgate+SWAP circuits, dynamical diagnostics and classical simulability can separate in both directions. In particular, the diagnostics can remain nontrivial after classical simulation becomes efficient, or become trivial before known efficient classical algorithms apply. We trace this mismatch to the different statistical properties they probe: magic and scrambling depend on fourth-order statistics of the Pauli spectrum, whereas the simulation algorithms depend primarily on second-order moments, which local noise suppresses at different rates. Thus, dynamical diagnostics measured on a noisy quantum device do not by themselves constitute evidence for classical hardness.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents advanced numerical algorithms for calculating electron overlap integrals required for quantum electronic structure simulations using Gausslet orbitals on a cubic lattice. By rigorously exploiting lattice symmetries, the authors achieve massive computational reductions in the number of integrals needed. This efficient methodology is demonstrated by accurately calculating the ground state energies of the hydrogen atom and molecule.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a highly optimized, scalable computational framework for quantum chemistry calculations, which is crucial for applying advanced electronic structure methods to larger, more complex molecular or solid-state systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is developing highly efficient algorithms to compute the necessary overlap integrals (kinetic, nuclear, and electron repulsion) for electronic structure simulations using Gausslet orbitals on cubic lattices.

**Main result.** The authors successfully developed symmetry-exploiting algorithms that drastically reduce the number of required electron repulsion integrals on a $5 	imes 5 	imes 5$ grid from $244$ million to under $330$ thousand, achieving rapid computation times.

**Method.** The methodology relies heavily on exploiting translational, permutation, and octahedral symmetries inherent in the Gausslet basis set to systematically reorder and precompute nested summations for the various integral types.

**Model / system.** The work focuses on electronic structure calculations using Gausslet orbitals defined on a cubic lattice ($\mathbb{Z}^3$). Demonstrations include calculating the ground state energy of the hydrogen atom and the hydrogen molecule.

**Key observables.** Overlap integrals ($k_{i,j}$, $nZ_{i,j}(R)$, $(ij|k\ell)$), ground state energy ($E_0$), and the rank of the resulting wavefunction coefficient matrix.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The grid size (e.g., $5 	imes 5 	imes 5$), the truncation tolerance ($10^{-5}$), and the scaling factor ($s$) used for basis set rescaling are key parameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary approximations include using the Integral Diagonal Approximation (IDA) for the electron repulsion integral tensor and assuming the factorized form of the Gausslet orbitals.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the asymptotic decay of ERIs, showing expected scaling, and show the ground state energy curves for the H atom and molecule as a function of the grid scaling factor $s$.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the physical problem and the Gausslet basis. It then details the mathematical derivation and reorganization of the three types of overlap integrals, heavily emphasizing the symmetry reduction techniques (Algorithm 1). Finally, it applies the developed framework to benchmark calculations for the H atom and H molecule.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Gausslet orbitals on a cubic lattice, introduced in [Steven R. White, J. Chem. Phys. 147, 244102 (2017)], represent a localized, smooth, and systematically refineable basis set featuring a "diagonal" approximability of the electron repulsion integral tensor. The present work develops efficient algorithms for evaluating overlap integrals required for electronic-structure simulations using these Gausslets, specifically the kinetic, nuclear, and electron repulsion integrals (both with and without the diagonal approximation). Computational efficiency improvements rest on the exploitation of translation, permutation, and octahedral symmetries, a reordering and precomputation of nested sums, as well as an early truncation of small coefficients. Our algorithms reduce the number of electron repulsion integrals on a $5 \times 5 \times 5$ grid from $125^4 = 244140625$ to $324275$ due to symmetries, and achieve a wall-clock runtime for evaluating the remaining integrals with a truncation tolerance of $10^{-5}$ in under 2 seconds on a laptop computer. We apply the developed methodology to compute the ground state of the hydrogen atom and molecule as a demonstration.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents an efficient quantum algorithm for the non-uniform Chebyshev transform (NUCT), overcoming limitations in previous quantum Fourier transform methods. By constructing a 'conditioning-free' NUQFT, the authors achieve a polylogarithmic gate complexity circuit for the NUCT. This advancement is significant for quantum simulation tasks requiring high-precision spectral analysis.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, resource-efficient quantum circuit implementation for a mathematically important transform (Chebyshev) that is critical in quantum simulation and spectral analysis, advancing the field of quantum signal processing.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing an efficient quantum algorithm for the non-uniform Chebyshev transform (NUCT), which is difficult because its sampling nodes are non-uniform in the angle $	heta$.

**Main result.** The authors provide an $\epsilon$-accurate block encoding of the NUCT matrix using $O(L)$ qubits and $\widetilde O(L^2)$ gates, where $L = \log N + \log(1/\epsilon)$, crucially removing dependence on geometry-dependent parameters from prior work.

**Method.** The NUCT is related to the average of two Type-II non-uniform DFTs, which are implemented using an improved, 'conditioning-free' Non-uniform Quantum Fourier Transform (NUQFT) circuit.

**Model / system.** The model involves quantum registers storing fixed-point numbers used to compute the transform coefficients based on Chebyshev polynomials sampled at specific nodes $x_k$.

**Key observables.** The output state fidelity and the circuit complexity in terms of qubits and gates.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The precision $\epsilon$, the transform size $N$, and the derived complexity parameter $L = \log N + \log(1/\epsilon)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the explicit construction of oracles for node and row access, and the equivalence of the NUCT to two Type-II NUDFTs.

**Figures summary.** Not specified.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the NUCT problem, improving the general NUQFT by removing $\kappa$ dependence, and finally applying this improved transform to construct the full NUCT circuit.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present an efficient quantum algorithm for the non-uniform Chebyshev transform. It is defined as the projection of a function onto Chebyshev polynomials sampled at given nodes that are uniform in $x\in[-1,1]$, and hence non-uniform in the angle $θ=\arccos x$, a setting that QFT-based quantum Chebyshev transforms cannot handle. Our construction is based on an improvement of an existing Non-uniform Quantum Fourier Transform (NUQFT) whereby we remove the conditioning from non-uniform node sampling. Hence, error bounds are independent of the geometry-dependent parameter $κ$ of prior work. We use the fact that Chebyshev transform matrix is the average of two Type-II non-uniform DFTs, which we implement with a single controlled NUQFT circuit. We provide explicit oracle constructions, including the row-access oracle previously left as an assumption. The resulting $\varepsilon$-accurate block encoding has $O(1)$ normalization and uses $O(L)$ qubits and $\widetilde O(L^2)$ gates, where $L=\log N+\log(1/\varepsilon)$. We give an end-to-end implementation with complexity analysis, including the success probability and output-state error.

</details>

**Model / system.** The model is quantum error correction, focusing on stabilizer codes and CSS codes defined over binary subspaces. The physical system involves encoding logical qubits into physical qubits to protect against errors while allowing selective gate operations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Recent work by Wills constructed codes with constant rate and transversal $T$. Extending this line of work, we construct asymptotically good CSS codes with \textbf{fully addressable} transversal $T$, permitting selective control over which logical qubits receive a $T$ gate. We also give Pauli-LDPC codes with transversal $T$ and growing distance at vanishing rate; and a protected-subsystem construction with fully addressable transversal $T$, constant protected rate, distance $Ω(\sqrt n)$, and sparse (non-Pauli) checks. More generally, we obtain asymptotically good binary codes with full transversal addressability for every fixed finite-order one-qubit gate, retaining CSS realizations for dyadic phase gates such as $\sqrt T$ and using generally nonadditive codes for rotations such as $R_z(π/7)$. The remaining challenge is to construct asymptotically good Pauli-LDPC codes with fully addressable transversal non-Clifford one-qubit gates.

**Summary.** This paper introduces a groundbreaking fault-tolerant scheme for quantum error correction that solves the problem of injecting and ejecting quantum states between physical qubits and encoded code blocks. By achieving constant space and time overhead, it significantly improves the feasibility of building large-scale quantum processors. The methodology relies on advanced code constructions using hypergraph products and rigorous gadget analysis.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides concrete, resource-efficient protocols for interfacing physical qubits with logical quantum memory, which is a critical bottleneck for scaling up quantum computation architectures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to construct a fault-tolerant method for injecting bare physical qubits into quantum error-correcting codes and subsequently ejecting encoded states back into physical qubits.

**Main result.** The authors present the first known fault-tolerant scheme achieving this injection/ejection with constant space and time overhead, succeeding under locally stochastic noise.

**Method.** The construction utilizes high-dimensional hypergraph products of classical LDPC codes, which are then concatenated to achieve resilience against uniform noise. Fault-tolerance is maintained via specialized 'gadgets' implemented with constant circuit depth.

**Model / system.** The system involves quantum error-correcting codes, specifically built using hypergraph products of classical LDPC codes derived from linear-time-encodable codes. The analysis is performed under the model of circuit-level locally stochastic noise.

**Key observables.** Logical error probability (bounded by a small constant for injection/ejection), constant space and time overhead ($O(1)$ depth).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The physical qubit count grows linearly with the number of logical qubits; the scheme assumes the ability to run polynomial-sized noiseless classical circuits.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The scheme assumes the availability of noiseless classical side-computations and that the physical qubits are exposed to a constant noise rate.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the process of code switching, showing the flow from one code block ($Q_1$) through an intermediate fault-tolerant block ($Q_2$) to an output block ($Q'_1$) using injection and ejection.

**Paper structure.** The paper follows a structure moving from motivation to technical overview, defining preliminaries, detailing the code construction via hypergraph products, presenting the decoder, and finally detailing the fault-tolerant gadgets and their rigorous proof of operation.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We construct the first known fault-tolerant scheme for injecting states into quantum error-correcting codes with constant space and time overhead. That is, we construct a family of constant-rate quantum error-correcting codes for which a set of bare physical qubits can be injected, i.e. fault-tolerantly encoded, into a code block. Similarly, a code state can be ejected, i.e. fault-tolerantly decoded, back into bare physical qubits. We show that these injection and ejection procedures succeed under circuit-level locally stochastic noise, while incurring just a small constant probability of corrupting each qubit, which is unavoidable for bare physical qubits. We also show how to perform fault-tolerant error correction and code-state preparation under locally stochastic noise. All of our gadgets can be implemented with constant quantum circuit depth (i.e. are single-shot), and with a number of physical qubits growing linearly with the number of logical qubits, assuming the ability to run polynomial-sized noiseless classical circuits on the side.   We construct our quantum codes by taking a high-dimensional hypergraph product of classical LDPC codes, which in turn are a simplified version of Spielman's linear-time encodable codes (STOC'95). As our resulting product codes are only resilient to physical errors occurring with non-uniform probabilities across qubits, we then show how to concatenate with inner codes of various sizes to obtain fault-tolerance against uniform noise.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously tests the assumption that minimizing the required EPR pair count is equivalent to minimizing the runtime in distributed quantum computing. By analyzing several benchmark circuits under varying communication conditions, the authors demonstrate that the two metrics are distinct, showing that minimum-EPR mappings can be suboptimal and that runtime differences are highly sensitive to communication latency and concurrency.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it provides critical theoretical constraints on resource estimation in large-scale quantum computation, guiding the development of more accurate compilation and scheduling tools for quantum hardware.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates whether the count of required EPR pairs (EPR cost) is a reliable proxy for the actual execution time in distributed quantum computing.

**Main result.** EPR cost and execution time are distinct optimization objectives; minimizing EPR cost does not guarantee minimum runtime, and the reliability of the proxy depends strongly on the specific quantum workload and communication operating regime.

**Method.** The authors systematically evaluate mappings of benchmark quantum circuits (QFT, QAOA, CDKM) onto two Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) by comparing the minimum EPR cost against the calculated distributed execution time under various concurrency models.

**Model / system.** The model simulates Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC) executing circuits across two interconnected QPUs. The complexity is analyzed by mapping circuits and calculating both the entanglement demand (EPR cost) and the runtime based on circuit dependencies (DAG scheduling).

**Key observables.** EPR Cost (CEPR), Distributed Execution Time (T_dist), Spearman's rank correlation ($ho_s$), Strict Rank Reversal Fraction (Frev), and Runtime Regret.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Circuit size ($N_q \in \{4, 6, 8, 10, 12\}$), EPR-generation latency ($ho_{	ext{EPR}}$), and communication concurrency limit ($N_{	ext{comm}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a baseline model where one EPR pair is consumed per non-local operation, ignoring entanglement reuse or advanced teleportation techniques.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the variation of the Strict Rank Reversal Fraction (Frev) across different circuits and qubit numbers, and show how the maximum runtime spread among equal-EPR mappings increases with EPR-generation latency.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem by comparing EPR cost to runtime across three benchmark circuits (QFT, QAOA, CDKM). It then systematically analyzes the relationship by varying communication latency and concurrency, concluding that explicit communication-aware runtime modeling is necessary.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

EPR-pair consumption is commonly used as a communication-cost objective in distributed quantum computing, but minimizing EPR cost does not necessarily minimize distributed execution time. Despite its widespread use, the reliability of EPR count as a runtime surrogate has received limited direct characterization across different workloads and communication conditions. This work addresses this gap by systematically evaluating the relationship between EPR cost and runtime over all balanced two-QPU mappings of QFT, QAOA, and CDKM circuits. The results show that mappings with identical EPR cost can have substantially different execution times, lower-EPR mappings can be slower, and minimum-EPR mappings can be runtime-suboptimal. The reliability of EPR count is strongly workload dependent and also changes with the communication operating regime: increasing EPR-generation latency amplifies runtime differences hidden by equal EPR cost, while increased communication concurrency can reduce the ability of EPR count to preserve runtime ordering. These results show that EPR count and execution time are related but distinct optimization objectives, and identify regimes in which explicit communication-aware runtime modeling is necessary.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously characterizes the equality conditions for the bosonic quantum entropy power inequality (qEPI) for independent inputs. It proves that saturation of this inequality requires the input quantum states to be Gaussian and possess identical covariance matrices. The methodology combines advanced techniques from quantum information theory, including doubling constructions and the quantum Darmois–Skitovich theorem.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous characterization of when fundamental entropy bounds are saturated in bosonic systems, linking information-theoretic inequalities directly to the Gaussian nature of the underlying quantum states, which is crucial for understanding quantum channels.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to determine the complete equality class for the bosonic quantum entropy power inequality (qEPI) for independent input states.

**Main result.** Equality in the qEPI (both linear and exponential forms) holds if and only if the input bosonic states are Gaussian and share the same covariance matrix.

**Method.** The proof uses a 'doubling construction' involving thermal auxiliary states, leading to an injectivity argument that forces the inputs to be product states, followed by applying the quantum Darmois–Skitovich theorem to establish Gaussianity.

**Model / system.** The system involves bosonic quantum modes (m-mode) interacting via a beam splitter with transmissivity $\eta$ ($0 < \eta < 1$), analyzing the relationship between input and output entropies.

**Key observables.** Von Neumann entropy ($S$), quantum relative entropy ($D$), and the entropy power inequality itself.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Transmissivity $\eta$ ($0 < \eta < 1$), finite mean photon number, and the covariance matrix of the input states.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The inputs $\rho_A, \rho_B$ are assumed to be independent, finite-energy $m$-mode states.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the 'doubled circuit' setup using beam splitters and auxiliary thermal states to facilitate the proof.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the proof by first analyzing the vanishing of entropy deficits ($L_C=0$ and $L_E=0$) via a doubling construction, which implies output independence. This leads to Gaussianity via the quantum Darmois–Skitovich theorem, and finally, a central-limit argument equates the exponential and linear forms.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The bosonic quantum entropy power inequality bounds the entropy of a beam-splitter output in terms of the input entropies. We determine its complete equality class among independent inputs of finite mean photon number: for any number of modes and any transmissivity strictly between zero and one, equality in either the linear or the exponential form holds if and only if the inputs are Gaussian with the same covariance matrix, allowing arbitrary displacements. The main step shows that equality for one output forces the two outputs to be independent: a thermal auxiliary converts equality into preservation of mutual information by a fixed noisy channel, and a two-outcome instrument shows that preservation of mutual information requires a product state with the reference. The quantum Darmois--Skitovich theorem then gives Gaussianity, while a central-limit argument reduces exponential equality to linear equality.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a method called 'exact diagonal completion' to simplify quantum circuits used in QAOA for placement problems by optimizing unused diagonal operator entries. Using weighted-$\ell_1$ optimization, the authors significantly reduced gate counts in simulations, demonstrating a powerful tool for quantum circuit compilation. However, the study concludes that while the circuit optimization is effective, it does not translate into a clear, end-to-end quantum advantage over classical solvers.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on quantum computation, the techniques for optimizing circuit structure via linear programming and sparse recurrence relations are mathematically rich and could inspire novel circuit optimization techniques applicable to other quantum information problems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates optimizing quantum circuits by performing 'exact diagonal completion' on unreachable subspaces, specifically applying this to the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for placement problems.

**Main result.** Weighted-$\ell_1$ completion successfully reduced Controlled-NOT (CX) counts in many tested geometries, though no end-to-end advantage was established over classical search methods in full integration.

**Method.** The authors construct exact Manhattan-distance operators using weighted-$\ell_1$ linear programming and a sparse recurrence relation to simplify the required quantum cost phases.

**Model / system.** The model involves quantum circuits used for solving placement problems, utilizing token permutation encoding and distance phases derived from weighted pairwise nets. The state preparation involves sequences of unitary operators.

**Key observables.** Controlled-NOT (CX) gate counts, circuit depth, and percentage reduction in gate counts compared to alternative circuit extensions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of sites (e.g., 6, 9, or 12 sites) and the structure of the underlying geometry (e.g., 160 geometries tested).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that optimizing unspecified diagonal entries on unreachable states does not alter the ideal computation, and the structured completion methods provide exact results for certain coordinate systems.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the prepared token circuit and the gate-level expansion of its mixer block using controlled register swaps. Other figures likely compare gate counts or circuit structures across different encoding methods.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by defining the problem (QAOA placement), developing the mathematical tools (weighted-$\ell_1$ completion, sparse recurrence), demonstrating the technique's efficacy through multiple simulations (160 geometries, 60-case cohort), and concluding with an integration study (OpenROAD) showing feasibility but limited quantum advantage.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Unused encoding states offer opportunities to simplify quantum circuits. For algorithms restricted to reachable subspaces, unspecified diagonal-operator entries can be optimized without changing ideal computation. We investigate exact diagonal completion for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) applied to placement, using permutation-preserving register swaps. We construct exact Manhattan-distance operators through weighted-$\ell_1$ optimization of Walsh coefficients and a sparse recurrence requiring $O(\sqrt{m})$ terms on balanced rectangles, avoiding $O(m^4)$ dense constraint storage.   Across 160 geometries, weighted-$\ell_1$ completion reduces controlled-NOT (CX) counts relative to four alternative extensions in all 96 cases with unused binary codes under Gray-code synthesis. On an independently specified 60-case cohort, median reductions relative to virtual-coordinate extension are 28.0\%, 53.9\%, and 21.6\% at six, nine, and twelve sites. Under generic diagonal synthesis, reductions decrease to 10.9\%, 1.3\%, and 0.7\%, demonstrating compiler dependence. Additional ancillas reduce mixer serialization, but token circuits remain deeper than one-hot baselines. Ideal placement simulations show baseline-dependent solution quality, with classical search performing better. OpenROAD integration takes 72 QAOA and 216 classical placements across six RTL designs through clock-tree synthesis and global routing with zero overflow. Completion improves phase construction; no end-to-end advantage is established.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a novel decoding algorithm, Rank-Decomposition Dynamic Programming (Rank DP), to calculate exact maximum-likelihood probabilities for quantum error correction. By exploiting the algebraic structure of the problem, it bypasses the exponential time complexity associated with standard tensor network contractions based on treewidth. This breakthrough allows for polynomial-time decoding for several important quantum codes, significantly advancing the field of quantum noise characterization.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a powerful algebraic tool (Rank DP) to tackle classically hard problems in quantum information theory, offering a path to simulating quantum error correction performance beyond the limits of standard tensor network contraction methods.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is computing the exact maximum-likelihood decoding probabilities for quantum error correction codes, which is computationally intractable due to exponential scaling with the treewidth of the associated tensor network.

**Main result.** The authors introduce Rank-Decomposition Dynamic Programming (Rank DP), an algorithm that evaluates the decoding partition function in time exponential only in the rank-width, which is superior to the standard treewidth-based contraction.

**Method.** The method reformulates the decoding problem as evaluating a partition function expressed as a quadratic sum of powers (SOPs) and applies Rank DP, which leverages the algebraic structure related to the rank-width of the Tanner graph.

**Model / system.** The work analyzes quantum error correction under stochastic Pauli noise, focusing on stabilizer codes like Reed-Muller and Steane-concatenated families. The complexity is analyzed using graph parameters like treewidth and rank-width.

**Key observables.** Decoding likelihoods (partition functions), conditional failure probabilities, and the comparison between computational complexities derived from rank-width versus treewidth.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The rank-width ($	ext{rw}$) of the Tanner graph, the noise model (stochastic Pauli noise), and the size of the code (e.g., up to 1,023 qubits for RM codes).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The approach assumes independent local fault factors for the Rank DP formulation, and the complexity bounds are derived within an arithmetic model.

**Figures summary.** The notes do not detail specific figures, but mention tables comparing failure probabilities and numerical enclosures for various codes and error rates.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops by first establishing the difficulty of exact MLD via TN contraction, then introducing the Rank DP framework by mapping the problem to SOPs, proving the complexity improvement using rank-width, and finally demonstrating its application to specific quantum codes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Maximum-likelihood decoding provides an optimal decoding strategy for quantum error correction under stochastic Pauli noise. However, computing logical-class probabilities is challenging, and the leading exact tensor-network contraction requires time exponential in treewidth. In this work, we introduce a new decoding algorithm based on rank-decomposition dynamic programming (Rank DP). We express decoding partition functions with independent local fault factors as quadratic sums of powers and apply Rank DP. The resulting exact evaluator has arithmetic complexity polynomial in the input size and exponential in the Tanner graph's rank-width with respect to the fault partition, including decomposition construction. After Gaussian elimination, it gives polynomial-time decoding for punctured quantum Reed-Muller codes and a Steane-concatenated family with growing distance under independent single-qubit Pauli noise. Standard contraction of the corresponding tensor networks requires superpolynomial time. A nonnegative realization gives relative floating-point error bounds under explicit arithmetic assumptions. Numerical experiments demonstrate runtime advantages over the tested tensor-network implementations on selected code-capacity and circuit-level instances, with full likelihood evaluation for Reed-Muller codes up to $1{,}023$ qubits. We further use these likelihoods to learn circuit noise parameters from syndromes, evaluate rare postselection probabilities, and quantify decoder optimality gaps. Our work opens new avenues for exploiting algebraic structure in quantum decoding and noise characterization.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper provides exact formulas for the spectral gaps associated with random Pauli rotations on both the special unitary group SU(d) and the projective unitary group PU(d). By combining graph theory, polynomial bounds, and representation theory, the authors disprove previous conjectures and establish rigorous bounds for quantum mixing processes.

**Why it may be interesting.** The precise determination of spectral gaps for random quantum circuits is crucial for understanding quantum error correction codes and the mixing time of quantum walks on quantum state spaces.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper resolves the spectral-gap problem for random Pauli rotations acting on the special unitary group SU(d) and the projective unitary group PU(d).

**Main result.** The exact spectral gap on SU(d) for n>=4 is found to be (d-8)/(8(d-1)), while the gap on PU(d) is shown to be d(d-3)/(8(d^2-1)).

**Method.** The analysis combines graph spectrum bounds from anticommuting Pauli operators, minimum-weight bounds for binary polynomials, and local inequalities on single-qubit subspaces.

**Model / system.** The model involves quantum evolution governed by random Pauli rotations, where the step is $e^{i	heta P}$, acting on a $d=2^n$ dimensional Hilbert space.

**Key observables.** The spectral gap $\Delta$, which measures the separation between the ground state energy and the first excited state energy.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of qubits $n$ (with regimes $n\ge3$ or $n\ge4$) and the dimension $d=2^n$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The proof is analytic and requires no computational verification, relying on specific algebraic structures related to Pauli operators and Clifford groups.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the gap on SU(d) using graph spectrum analysis, then addresses the gap on PU(d) by relating it to the conjectured formula, and finally uses advanced representation theory (exterior powers, highest-weight vectors) to confirm the results.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We resolve the spectral-gap problem posed by Baer and Haah for random Pauli rotations. In this walk, a nonidentity $n$-qubit Pauli operator $P$ and an angle $θ$ modulo $2π$ are chosen independently and uniformly, and the step is $e^{\mathrm{i}θP}$. Writing $d=2^n$, we prove that the gap on $\mathsf{SU}(d)$ is $(d-8)/(8(d-1))$ for $n\ge4$. This disproves their conjectured formula on the full special unitary group. We also prove that the conjectured value, $d(d-3)/(8(d^2-1))$, is exactly the gap on $\mathsf{PU}(d)$ for $n\ge3$. The special-unitary gap is attained by an explicit vector in $\bigwedge^8\mathbb C^d$, constructed from affine three-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb F_2^n$. Its nontrivial central action explains why balanced tensor representations do not detect this smaller gap. On the projective group, the gap is attained in $U\mapsto U^{\otimes4}\otimes\bar U^{\otimes4}$. The matching lower bounds hold uniformly over all finite-dimensional unitary representations. They combine the spectrum of the graph of anticommuting Pauli operators, a minimum-weight bound for binary polynomials, and a local inequality on a single-qubit Clifford-fixed subspace. The proof is analytic and requires no computational verification.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents the first explicit construction of quantum LDPC codes that achieve list decoding capacity. The codes are built using expander graphs via quantum AEL amplification, and the authors develop a corresponding near-linear time decoding algorithm. This advances the field by providing highly structured, efficient quantum error-correcting codes.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work pushes the boundaries of quantum error correction by combining the desirable LDPC structure with capacity-achieving list decoding guarantees, which is crucial for practical quantum computation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To construct explicit quantum Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes that achieve list decoding capacity and are decodable in near-linear time.

**Main result.** The authors provide the first explicit construction of such quantum LDPC codes, achieving a list decoding radius approaching the quantum Singleton bound with constant list sizes.

**Method.** The construction utilizes expander graphs via the quantum analogue of Alon-Edmonds-Luby (AEL) amplification, and the decoding algorithm generalizes classical weak-regularity list decoding techniques.

**Model / system.** The work operates in the framework of quantum error correction, specifically constructing CSS codes defined over finite fields, which are characterized by their LDPC structure.

**Key observables.** List decoding radius ($	au_N$), code rate ($R_N$), list size ($\ell$), and decoding time complexity.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Block length ($N$), list size ($\ell = O(1/\epsilon)$), and the required rate $R$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the existence of suitable expander graphs and the ability to solve local Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs) efficiently.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from the general problem statement to the explicit construction using qAEL codes, followed by the development of a near-linear time decoding algorithm based on solving local CSPs and outer stitching.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In classical coding theory, the quest for explicit codes achieving list decoding capacity has been an important driving force. While random codes are easily shown to achieve capacity, an explicit construction was only discovered decades later in the seminal work [Guruswami and Rudra, STOC 2006]. In quantum coding theory, it is highly desirable that a code family be LDPC. While good quantum codes were known for decades, obtaining the additional LDPC property was elusive. In fact, only very recently that good quantum LDPC codes were discovered in a breakthrough work [Panteleev and Kalachev, STOC 2022].   In this context, a natural question is to ask for an explicit family of quantum codes achieving list decoding capacity while also possessing the important LDPC property. In this work, we provide (to the best of our knowledge) the first explicit constructions of quantum LDPC codes achieving list decoding capacity, namely, with a list decoding radius approaching the quantum Singleton bound with constant list sizes. Furthermore, we provide near-linear time (in the block-length) list decoding algorithms approaching capacity.   Our explicit code construction are based on expander graphs via the quantum analogue of Alon-Edmonds-Luby (AEL) amplification [Bergamaschi, Golowich and Gunn, STOC 2024], and this enables the important LDPC property. Our efficient list decoding algorithms are obtained by generalizing the classical expander-based weak-regularity list decoding algorithms [Srivastava and Tulsiani, FOCS 2025] [Jeronimo and Singh, 2025] to suitable instantiations of quantum AEL.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To establish the first exponential quantum advantage in the general interactive three-party Numbers-on-Forehead (NOF) model for a decision problem.

**Main result.** The authors achieve an exponential separation for the Interleaved Unitary Product (IUP) problem, showing an $O(\log n)$ quantum communication requirement versus $\Omega(n^{1/32})$ classical communication.

**Method.** The separation is achieved by combining a quantum upper bound protocol and a novel regularity-based argument for randomized classical lower bounds, adapting advanced decomposition techniques.

**Model / system.** The model is the three-party Numbers-on-Forehead (NOF) communication setting, applied to the Interleaved Unitary Product (IUP) problem. The quantum protocol operates in the one-clean-qubit communication model.

**Key observables.** The communication complexity (qubits vs. bits) required to solve the IUP function, and the expectation values related to unitary products.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The input size $n$, the communication complexity $O(\log n)$ (quantum) vs. $\Omega(n^{1/32})$ (classical), and the dimension $m$ of the underlying matrices.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The quantum protocol assumes the one-clean-qubit model. The lower bound relies on advanced regularity decomposition techniques and the ability to approximate measurable cylinder intersections.

**Figures summary.** Not specified in the notes, but the structure suggests proofs involving bounds on expectations and decomposition procedures.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds by first defining the problem (IUP in 3-party NOF), then establishing the quantum upper bound using controlled operations, and finally deriving the classical lower bound using regularity decomposition arguments adapted from prior work.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We give the first exponential quantum advantage in the general interactive three-party Numbers-on-Forehead (NOF) model for a decision problem. Previous separations hold only for restricted protocols like one-way communication for a relation. We construct an explicit partial Boolean function, the Interleaved Unitary Product problem, that requires only $O(\log n)$ NOF quantum communication but $\widetildeΩ(n^{1/32})$ randomized communication. This function builds on the two-party unitary product problem of Arunachalam, Girish, and Lifshitz (TQC 2024).   The main technical obstacle is that discrepancy, the standard lower-bound method for NOF, also lower-bounds quantum communication. We instead develop a regularity-based argument for randomized NOF lower bounds, building on the approach of Kelley, Lovett, and Meka and adapting the regularity decomposition of Abboud, Fischer, Kelley, Lovett, and Meka (STOC 2024) to cylinder intersections. Combined with matrix-product estimates of Arunachalam, Girish, and Lifshitz, this yields our randomized lower bound.

</details>

**Why it may be interesting.** While the topic is cryptography/QIP, the rigorous analysis of computational thresholds and the explicit comparison of quantum vs. classical scaling laws are highly relevant to understanding the limits of quantum computation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper analyzes the computational difficulty of the $\mathbb{F}_3^n$-Subset-Sum problem and the related Binary-Error Learning-with-Errors (LWE) problem.

**Main result.** The authors present quantum algorithms suggesting an exponential quantum speedup for Subset-Sum when the number of vectors $m$ is small relative to $n^2$, and they establish deterministic classical algorithms for LWE.

**Method.** The work combines quantum algorithm design, rigorous analysis of sample-time tradeoffs, and the application of advanced algebraic techniques like Degree-3 XL attacks.

**Model / system.** The analysis is purely computational, focusing on algebraic problems defined over finite fields ($\mathbb{F}_3$ and $\mathbb{F}_q$). The underlying structure relates to lattice problems and cryptographic hardness assumptions.

**Key observables.** The primary observables are the required number of input vectors ($m$) relative to the dimension ($n$) needed to solve the problem efficiently.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The critical parameters are the field size (3 or $q$), the dimension $n$, and the ratio $m/n$ which determines the complexity regime.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on establishing sample-time tradeoffs, some of which are noted to depend on unproven regularity assumptions, and the quantum speedup claims are conditional on these algorithmic breakthroughs.

**Figures summary.** No specific figure summaries were extracted, but the notes detail comparisons between quantum, classical, and previous state-of-the-art bounds for various parameter regimes.

**Paper structure.** The paper is structured around comparing the quantum and classical complexity bounds for Subset-Sum and LWE. It moves from general theoretical results (Theorem 1.3) to specific deterministic classical attacks (Theorem 1.7) and concludes with phase transition analysis using probability inequalities.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study vector subset sum over $\mathbb{F}_3^n$: given $m$ random vectors from $\mathbb{F}_3^n$, find a nonempty subset that sums to zero; the smaller $m$, the more difficult it is to find such a subset. Chen, Liu, and Zhandry (EUROCRYPT'22) introduced an efficient quantum algorithm that solves this problem when $m\approx n^2/2$, where a naive classical algorithm would require exponential time. Subsequently, Kothari, O'Donnell, and Wu (STOC'2026) gave an efficient classical algorithm that only requires $m \approx n^2/3$ vectors, thus removing the hope for an exponential quantum advantage in this parameter regime.   Using the framework of Chen, Liu, and Zhandry, we give quantum algorithms that require much fewer input vectors, renewing the possibility of an exponential quantum speedup: for any fixed $ε>0$, our quantum algorithm solves $\mathbb{F}_3$-subset sum in polynomial time with $m=ε\cdot n^2$ vectors. More generally, we establish a full sample--time tradeoff that interpolates between exponential and polynomial runtime.   The main ingredient is a deterministic classical algorithm for the binary-error Learning-with-Errors problem, which is of independent cryptographic interest. For this, we rigorously establish a sample--time tradeoff that was predicted by earlier algebraic heuristics. For vector subset sums over larger fields, we also significantly improve classical algorithms in Kothari, O'Donnell, and Wu (STOC'2026).

</details>

**Summary.** This paper demonstrates that the computational depth of Clifford circuits can be maintained at an optimal $O(\log n)$ scaling even when using only 'catalytic' qubits instead of clean ancillas. By employing algebraic cancellation techniques, the authors show that this catalytic memory approach is sufficient for implementing complex quantum operations efficiently. This advances the understanding of resource trade-offs in quantum circuit design.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful theoretical tool for resource-constrained quantum computation, showing how to achieve optimal depth scaling without requiring perfect, clean quantum memory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates replacing the need for clean (known initial state) ancillary qubits in quantum circuits with 'catalytic' qubits, which must have their joint state restored at the end of the computation.

**Main result.** They show that every $n$-qubit Clifford circuit can be implemented catalytically with depth $O(\log n)$ using $O(n^2 / \log^2 n)$ catalytic qubits, matching the best achievable depth.

**Method.** The authors use algebraic cancellation techniques, building on the Clifford normal form, to eliminate the dependence on the unknown initial state of the catalytic qubits.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on quantum circuits, specifically Clifford circuits and diagonal unitaries belonging to the Clifford hierarchy ($C_k$). The model distinguishes between clean ancillas (starting in $|0angle$) and catalytic ancillas (starting in an arbitrary state $|	auangle$).

**Key observables.** Depth of the circuit (e.g., $O(\log n)$), required number of catalytic qubits (e.g., $O(n^2 / \log^2 n)$), and the absence of clean qubits.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Number of qubits ($n$), the level of the Clifford hierarchy ($k$), and the depth scaling factor ($\log n$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The results are established for Clifford and semi-Clifford circuits; the conjecture for general quantum circuits remains open.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the catalytic implementation for general Clifford circuits, then extending the technique to diagonal elements of the Clifford hierarchy, and finally addressing semi-Clifford gates, always aiming to maintain logarithmic depth scaling.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Additional qubits can reduce the depth of a quantum circuit by providing workspace for parallel computation, but standard constructions assume that this workspace is initialized in a known state. In this work we study catalytic implementations, i.e. asking whether dirty qubits can instead be used provided that their joint state including any entanglement with other registers is restored exactly at the end of the computation. We show that every $n$-qubit Clifford circuit has a catalytic implementation of depth $O(\log n)$ using $O(n^2/\log^2 n)$ catalytic qubits and no clean qubits, matching the asymptotic depth achievable when clean workspace is available. We extend this approach to diagonal elements of any fixed level $C_k$ of the Clifford hierarchy, which admit catalytic implementations of depth $O(\log(n+1))$ with $O(n^k/\log(n))$ gates and $O(n^k/\log^2(n))$ catalytic qubits, as well as to semi-Clifford Gates.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes the fault-tolerant resource cost of running shallow QAOA circuits on structured optimization problems. By employing small-angle rotation synthesis, the required non-Clifford gate cost is significantly reduced to $eO(n^2)$. This analysis confirms the exponential quantum speedup while providing critical resource estimates necessary for hardware implementation.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides concrete, resource-aware estimates for running quantum algorithms on near-term, noisy hardware, which is crucial for designing feasible quantum simulations or quantum advantage demonstrations.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper determines the fault-tolerant resource cost required to execute shallow Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) circuits for solving near-symmetric optimization problems.

**Main result.** Small-angle synthesis reduces the non-Clifford gate cost per circuit to $eO(n^2)$, enabling the study of larger problems while maintaining an exponential speedup over classical solvers.

**Method.** The analysis uses small-angle Clifford+T rotation synthesis and compares resource scaling across different circuit decomposition methods (quasi-probability vs. probability mixture).

**Model / system.** The model is fault-tolerant quantum computation implemented on a surface-code-based architecture, using QAOA circuits to solve constraint satisfaction problems.

**Key observables.** Success Probability ($\Omega(1)$), Non-Clifford Cost ($eO(n^2)$), Degree-one Fourier coefficients ($h_i$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Locality ($\ell$), Sparsification fraction ($f$), Phase-matched angle ($\gamma = \Theta(n^{1-\ell})$), Time limit (one-hour cap).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a surface-code-based fault-tolerant architecture and relies on the small-angle approximation holding true.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the cost reduction from the value-oracle model to the explicit clause list, showing the $eO(n^2)$ cost. Figure 2 compares the scaling of the non-Clifford cost for different QAOA depths and synthesis conventions.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from establishing the empirical speedup of low-depth QAOA, derives the small-angle scaling required for success, calculates the resulting fault-tolerant gate cost using advanced synthesis techniques, and finally discusses resource limitations imposed by hardware constraints.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Montanaro and Zhou proved that depth-one Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) finds the planted solution of certain near-symmetric constraint satisfaction problems with probability $Ω(1)$, and observed exponential runtimes for general-purpose classical solvers on explicit realizations, providing strong evidence of an empirical exponential speedup of low-depth QAOA. We ask what such a circuit costs fault-tolerantly. Although the cost Hamiltonian carries $Θ(n^\ell)$ clauses, the rotation angle at which QAOA succeeds shrinks as $n^{1-\ell}$, and we show that small-angle Clifford$+T$ rotation synthesis reduces the non-Clifford cost per circuit to $\widetilde O(n^2)$ for every clause locality $\ell$. Compiling the circuit, however, requires the explicit clause list. We find that the mechanism underlying constant QAOA success fixes the degree-one Fourier coefficients of the cost, whose signs reveal the planted solution. However, this leakage need not reveal the solution: we design families in which the quadratic non-Clifford scaling and hard exact optimization coexist.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper tackles the challenge of finding explicit quantum error-correcting codes that achieve the optimal performance bounds known for random quantum codes. By developing a quantum version of the LCL framework, the authors establish theoretical thresholds and provide concrete, explicit constructions for quantum list-decodable and list-recoverable codes. These resulting codes are all of the desirable qLDPC type.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous mathematical bridge between the theoretical existence of optimal quantum codes (random codes) and the practical requirement of having explicit, structured codes (qLDPC codes), which is crucial for building physical quantum hardware.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central goal is to construct explicit quantum error-correcting codes, specifically qLDPC codes, whose optimal properties match those of theoretically ideal random quantum codes.

**Main result.** The authors provide explicit constructions for quantum list-decodable and list-recoverable codes with optimal list sizes, all of which are proven to be qLDPC codes.

**Method.** They develop a quantum analogue of the Local Coordinate-wise Linear (LCL) framework for nested quantum spaces, adapting the Alon–Edmonds–Luby (AEL) local-to-global paradigm to derandomize theoretical guarantees into concrete constructions.

**Model / system.** The work focuses on quantum error correction codes, particularly CSS quantum codes, analyzed using the qLCL framework for nested subspaces $S \subseteq C$. The underlying structure involves stabilizer codes and their logical quotients.

**Key observables.** Code parameters (rate, distance, list sizes), quantum ranks (physical vs. logical), and threshold values for decoding.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The construction depends on achieving optimal list sizes and maintaining the qLDPC structure, relating to the rate $R$ and error parameters $ho$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The theory relies on adapting classical coding-theoretic tools (like LCL witnesses) to the quantum setting, and the final constructions assume the existence of explicit outer CSS families with desired properties.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds theory by introducing the quantum-LCL framework, deriving threshold theorems for random CSS codes, defining quantum subspace designs, and culminating in explicit constructions for various quantum list-decodable/recoverable properties.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Constructing explicit codes matching the parameters of random codes has been a central and largely elusive question in coding theory. The quantum setting is even more challenging since it is highly desirable that the quantum code be an LDPC code.   Local coordinate-wise linear (LCL) [Levi, Mosheiff, and Shagrithaya, FOCS 2025] witnesses provide a unifying language for many coding-theoretic properties, from distance to list decoding and list recovery. In particular, it provides a framework to study properties of random linear codes, which achieve optimal parameters for many properties of linear codes.   For CSS quantum codes, however, a local witness has two distinct ranks: its physical rank before quotienting by stabilizers and its logical rank after quotienting. We develop a quantum version of the LCL framework for nested spaces $S \subseteq C$, in which local constraints are imposed on physical representatives while independence is measured in the logical quotient $C/S$. The resulting theory gives a threshold theorem for random CSS codes, and as a consequence shows that the per-sector rate threshold is equal to the classical rate threshold. We also define a quantum analogue of subspace design [Guruswami and Xing, STOC 2013] and show that they can be described in a natural manner within the quantum-LCL framework.   Finally, we give explicit constructions for arbitrary folded quantum-LCL properties, in a manner similar to the LCL derandomization of [Jeronimo and Shagrithaya, STOC 2026]. As a consequence, we obtain the first explicit constructions of quantum list-decodable codes and list-recoverable codes that have optimal list sizes, in addition to explicit quantum subspace design codes. We note that all our explicit constructions are qLDPC codes, an important property for quantum error-correcting codes.

</details>
